# Unity Catalog Volumes: Unstructured Data for the Agentic Lakehouse

URL: https://www.unitycatalog.io/blogs/uc-volumes/
Republished at: https://openlakehouse.io/blog/unity-catalog/uc-volumes
Original publisher: Unity Catalog
Date: 2026-11-10
Category: Unity Catalog

import img0 from "./remote-storage-panel.png";

<Callout type="info" title="TL;DR">
  - Unity Catalog Volumes provide a powerful abstraction for governing and processing unstructured data.
  - A volume opens as an obstore store in a marimo notebook, with credentials Unity Catalog vends for that one volume.
  - Volumes are a fundamental building block for rich user experiences and storage-based services.
  - Much of an agent's context, such as instruction files and LLM wikis, is files by convention, and a volume gives those files a governed home.
</Callout>

The usage of object stores as the storage layer for all kinds of data systems
has been on a continuous rise for several years. For analytical workloads, separated
storage and compute - a key concept of the Lakehouse Architecture - is the de-facto
standard, and even some transactional workloads are following suit.

And while we as a community made great strides managing and governing tabular assets
in object storage via catalogs and open table formats, we always kept an escape hatch around.
This escape hatch is plain storage; data pipelines read configuration files, data scientists
develop ideas as scratch files in some personal storage location, and many more examples
where folks need to quickly park something for later use or reference. Even more promiently,
the usage of multimodal data (e.g. images, PDFs, videos...) is skyrocketing with the proloferation
of agentic workloads.

Those of you building or using data platforms frequently, will already anticipate the issues
arising from such patterns: missing discoverability and fragmented governance. You will also
recognize these as challenges we already encountered and solved for tabular assets,
particularly those based on open table formats.

In the following sections we will explore how Unity Catalog leverages well-established abstractions
and capabilities to define a Volume securable, and see how Volumes can be leveraged to
govern and process unstructured data.

## Accessing volumes from a notebook

Say you want to browse a volume from a notebook. [marimo](https://marimo.io)
lists every [obstore](https://developmentseed.org/obstore/) store a notebook defines in its
[Remote Storage panel](https://docs.marimo.io/guides/working_with_data/remote_storage/), where
you can browse and download files. Give that store a credential provider that asks Unity Catalog
for credentials, and you can open a volume as a store. That provider is small enough to show in full:

```python title="obstore_credentials.py" srcpath="content/unitycatalog/how-to/023-obstore-credentials/snippets/obstore_credentials.py" srcstart="47" srcregion="start:provider..end:provider"
class UnityCatalogCredentials:
    """An obstore credential provider that asks Unity Catalog for storage credentials.

    It returns whichever credential the server vends: S3 keys, an Azure SAS
    token, or a Google Cloud OAuth token. `request` is an async function that
    takes an `ApiClient` and returns the server's `TemporaryCredentials`. It
    runs on an event loop of its own, in a background thread, so obstore can
    call the provider from sync methods, async methods, and threads without a
    loop alike.
    """

    def __init__(self, config, request):
        self._request = request
        self._loop = asyncio.new_event_loop()
        threading.Thread(target=self._loop.run_forever, daemon=True).start()
        self._api = self._run(self._connect(config))
        # The first answer gives the store its URL, and a missing grant fails here.
        self._first = self._run(request(self._api))
        self.url = self._first.url

    @classmethod
    def for_volume(cls, config, name, operation=VolumeOperation.READ_VOLUME):
        async def request(api):
            volume = await VolumesApi(api).get_volume(name=name)
            return await TemporaryCredentialsApi(
                api
            ).generate_temporary_volume_credentials(
                GenerateTemporaryVolumeCredential(
                    volume_id=volume.volume_id, operation=operation
                )
            )

        return cls(config, request)

    @classmethod
    def for_table(cls, config, full_name, operation=TableOperation.READ):
        async def request(api):
            table = await TablesApi(api).get_table(full_name=full_name)
            return await TemporaryCredentialsApi(
                api
            ).generate_temporary_table_credentials(
                GenerateTemporaryTableCredential(
                    table_id=table.table_id, operation=operation
                )
            )

        return cls(config, request)

    @classmethod
    def for_path(cls, config, url, operation=PathOperation.PATH_READ):
        async def request(api):
            return await TemporaryCredentialsApi(
                api
            ).generate_temporary_path_credentials(
                GenerateTemporaryPathCredential(url=url, operation=operation)
            )

        return cls(config, request)

    @staticmethod
    async def _connect(config):
        return ApiClient(config)

    def _run(self, coroutine):
        return asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(coroutine, self._loop).result()

    def __call__(self):
        creds = self._first or self._run(self._request(self._api))
        self._first = None
        # expiration_time is in epoch milliseconds.
        expires_at = datetime.fromtimestamp(creds.expiration_time / 1000, tz=UTC)
        if aws := creds.aws_temp_credentials:
            return {
                "access_key_id": aws.access_key_id,
                "secret_access_key": aws.secret_access_key,
                "token": aws.session_token,
                "expires_at": expires_at,
            }
        if azure := creds.azure_user_delegation_sas:
            return {"sas_token": azure.sas_token, "expires_at": expires_at}
        if gcp := creds.gcp_oauth_token:
            return {"token": gcp.oauth_token, "expires_at": expires_at}
        raise ValueError(f"the server vended no credential for {creds.url}")

    def close(self):
        self._run(self._api.close())
        self._loop.call_soon_threadsafe(self._loop.stop)


```

obstore calls the provider whenever it needs a credential, and each call goes back to
Unity Catalog for a fresh one. The first answer also carries the volume's storage location, which becomes the
store's URL. With that in place, this is the cell that opens the volume:

```python title="notebook.py" srcpath="content/unitycatalog/how-to/024-marimo-remote-storage/snippets/notebook.py" srcstart="194" srcregion="start:nb-store..end:nb-store"
credentials = UnityCatalogCredentials.for_volume(config, "analytics.ops.files")
files = from_url(
    credentials.url, region="us-east-1", credential_provider=credentials
)
```

Once the cell runs, the volume shows up under **Remote Storage** in the **Files** panel:

<Figure src={img0} alt="Screenshot: marimo's Files panel, where the Remote Storage section lists the files store as Amazon S3 at the volume's storage location, with the volume's reports folder underneath." />

Other cells read through the same store with plain obstore calls. There are no storage keys anywhere
in the notebook. The store knows the volume's name, and Unity Catalog
answers with the volume's storage location and a credential scoped to it.

The governance comes along for free. `for_volume` asks for `READ_VOLUME`, so the store can list
and read, and storage itself rejects writes. Writing from a cell means asking for `WRITE_VOLUME`,
which needs ownership of the volume. obstore renews the credential once less than five
minutes remain, so a long-running notebook keeps working, and since every renewal goes back to
the server, revoking the grant also cuts off a notebook that is already open.

Nothing in `UnityCatalogCredentials` is specific to marimo. Any tool that accepts an obstore store gets the same volume, with the same grants.
[Use volumes as marimo remote storage](https://docs.unitycatalog.io/how-to/marimo-remote-storage)
walks through the whole notebook, and
[Use Unity Catalog credentials with obstore](https://docs.unitycatalog.io/how-to/obstore-credentials)
explains the provider, including how it serves table files and handles S3, Azure, and Google Cloud
credentials.

## What makes a volume

So what is it that we just opened? Let's take a more formal look at what Volumes in Unity Catalog are and what
metadata we associate with them.

```json title="volume.json" srcpath="blogs/uc-volumes/volume.json" srcstart="1"
{
  "name": "string",
  "catalog_name": "string",
  "schema_name": "string",
  "volume_type": "string",
  "storage_location": "string",
  "owner": "string",
  "comment": "string",
  "full_name": "string",
  "volume_id": "string",
  "metastore_id": "string",
  "created_at": 0,
  "created_by": "string",
  "updated_at": 0,
  "updated_by": "string",
  "access_point": "string",
  "browse_only": true
}
```

The first thing to note is that Volumes are a first class data asset organized within
the catalog/schema hierarchy. As such they are governed and discoverable just like other assets.
In the same vein, you can supply comments to clarify the intended use of a volume.

The most relevant piece of information though is the storage location. This can be any path under
a previously registered external location or automatically created when the location is `MANAGED`
by Unity Catalog. Using the same [credential vending](https://docs.unitycatalog.io/explanation/credential-vending)
mechanics we already employ for tables via the
[temporary credential APIs](https://docs.unitycatalog.io/how-to/temporary-credentials)
and of course the Unity Catalog Delta API and IRC protocol implementation in UC, we have battle-tested
abstractions to negotiate access to volumes. That is exactly the API the marimo store calls.

## From one notebook to a platform

As we see, using storage credentials, external (or managed) locations, and a path, we have defined
a Volume abstraction. While this already solves a lot of the aforementioned discoverability and
governance issues we identified, it is worthwhile to take a step back and step into the shoes
of someone designing and building an on-prem data platform. What key experiences does this person
want to offer their users?

Going out on a limb here, but likely users expect some sort of notebook environment and maybe
a SQL editor experience to interact with the data stored on the platform. The marimo panel above
is the read side of that story. The other side is that notebooks themselves usually manifest as
some sort of file, be it `.ipynb`, `.json`, or plain `.py` files. In case of a SQL editor, you might
want to persist state not only in the browser, but make it resumable and shareable by storing it
as a `.sql` file. In fact embedding a text editor to display and edit SQL will get you a long way
towards an incredibly rich editing experience.

By introducing system schemas and/or injected configuration into existing tooling, platform
engineers can leverage volumes to build such file-centric experiences with discoverability
and governance built in from the ground up, not as an additional application-specific
layer bolted on after the fact. Injecting a credential provider into a notebook kernel, so every
user's notebook sees the volumes they are granted and nothing else, is one such integration point.

But that is not all.

## Volumes as AI primitive

In today's world no platform story is complete without agents and AI as primary interfaces.
So why are we boring you with plain old storage when there are so many more exciting things
to talk about? Well, if we look under the hood, much of what we hand to an agent is just
instructions (usually markdown files) along with file-based resources and scripts referenced
in these instructions.

Take [AGENTS.md](https://agents.md), a convention for telling coding agents how to work in a
project: a markdown file at a well-known path, pointing at whatever else the agent should read.
Nothing about it requires a git repository. Put the instructions and their references into a
volume, and its owner decides who can read them, with the same `READ_VOLUME` privilege that
already governs their data. An agent then reads its
context through the same vended credentials the notebook above uses. The files an agent
produces, such as reports or generated notebooks, can land in a volume the same way, and the
`WRITE_VOLUME` check applies to the agent just as it does to a person.

Beyond extending the abilities of your agents via such direct integrations, the community at large
is also hard at work to provide a semantic layer on top of the Lakehouse. And while this is an
expansive and evolving field including the recently announced
[metric view](https://unitycatalog.io/blogs/uc-metric-views/) support in Unity Catalog,
by now you might not be surprised to learn that Volumes are again a great primitive to
build part of your semantic layer.

The idea of an [LLM-wiki](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f)
quickly gained traction, and got formalized via the [Open Knowledge Format](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/data-analytics/how-the-open-knowledge-format-can-improve-data-sharing).
By design this is a very lightweight specification, with the only hard requirement to put a
`type` field into the frontmatter of a markdown file.

Again we see that the fundamental building block is ultimately files. The power comes from the
well known UX concept of [progressive disclosure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_disclosure),
which just so happens to align nicely with how we want to populate agent context, loading
only the pieces into context that are relevant to the task at hand. Individual pages of such a
wiki along with the relations to other concepts in the knowledge graph can effectively be shared
using the OpenSharing protocol, particularly [pages](https://github.com/OpenSharing-IO/OpenSharing/blob/main/spec/protocols/GLOSSARY.md).

## Wrapping Up

Every now and then we come across concepts that seem obvious in retrospect
and are simple yet incredibly powerful upon closer examination. To me,
volumes are just that, a governed, secured, and discoverable storage location
that provides significant value on its own, and serves as a key building
block for a wide range of use cases across AI, agents, and platform engineering.

If you want to try it yourself, these pages from the Unity Catalog docs get you there:

- [Manage volumes](https://docs.unitycatalog.io/how-to/manage-volumes) to create a
  volume and see which privileges reading it takes.
- [Working with volumes and files](https://docs.unitycatalog.io/tutorials/read-volume-files)
  to register a folder of documents as a volume and read it knowing only its name.
- [Use volumes as marimo remote storage](https://docs.unitycatalog.io/how-to/marimo-remote-storage)
  for the notebook from this post.
- [Use Unity Catalog credentials with obstore](https://docs.unitycatalog.io/how-to/obstore-credentials)
  to take the same credential provider into your own tools.

Go build!

---

*This post was originally published on the [Unity Catalog blog](https://www.unitycatalog.io/blogs/uc-volumes/) by Robert Pack.*

# A Field Guide to Apache Iceberg 1.12

URL: https://datacircus.substack.com/p/a-field-guide-to-apache-iceberg-112
Republished at: https://openlakehouse.io/blog/iceberg/iceberg-1-12-field-guide
Original publisher: Distributed Thoughts
Date: 2026-10-01
Category: Iceberg

*Originally published on [Distributed Thoughts](https://datacircus.substack.com/p/a-field-guide-to-apache-iceberg-112), Scott Haines's Substack.*

Anyone who has lived through a home renovation knows the gap between what looks like progress and what actually is progress. There is scaffolding across the front of the house, a permit taped to the window, and framing going up for a new addition that won’t be ready until next year. Meanwhile, it seems that every week there is another unexpected roadblock or unknown unknown. The addition is what we tell people about. The work that went into it rarely is.

Apache Iceberg 1.12 is part of the Table Format V4 renovation. There is an enormous amount of visible framing going up with roughly forty pull requests touching V4 internals, but just like a renovation in progress, we simply can’t use any of it yet. The work that will actually change our lives is behind the scenes: a cluster of bugs that were returning wrong answers without telling anyone, a real solution to Flink’s equality-delete problem, and Variant finally gaining the speedup we all knew it was capable of.

So, without further ado, let’s take a look at the 1.12 release: what’s new, what’s been fixed, and, more specifically, what to upgrade for, what to check before we upgrade, and which features are releasing with a little bit of red tape.

## The Road to V4

There are roughly forty pull requests in this release touching V4 internals. `TrackedFile` is the unified manifest entry that collapses the `DataFile`/`DeleteFile` split that defined Iceberg until now. [Relative paths](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15630) land in the spec with [resolution in the V4 manifest reader](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17434), and for anyone who has ever wanted to simplify copying a table from one location to another, this is the light at the end of the V4 tunnel. [Content stats](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14234) were also merged, with a genuinely elegant compatibility bridge living within `ContentStatsBackedMap` that presents typed columnar stats to a decade of existing code as the legacy bounds map, lazily, allocating nothing on point reads.

So can we use V4? The short answer is “not at this point.” It is also worth pointing out that V4 and adaptive metadata trees are not synonymous.

The adaptive metadata tree (AMT) replaces manifest lists with a small root manifest, inlines small commits, and provides a tree shape that adapts to each workload. This work is in progress and isn’t ready for prime time: at the time of writing, the read path itself is still not wired into place, with the V4 scan task planner still sitting in an open pull request. The write-direction wrappers are also still open, with changes requested as recently as September. The spec itself says Version 4 is under active development and has not been formally adopted.

What 1.12 contains is the **vocabulary** of V4: the entry struct, typed statistics, relative paths, manifest encoding, and the compatibility bridges. What is missing is the adaptive metadata tree, a scan that can traverse it, and a committer that can build it. It is simply not a feature we can turn on at this point in time.

It is tempting to say V4 is safely gated off. It is not. On main, `TableMetadata` carries:

```java
static final int SUPPORTED_TABLE_FORMAT_VERSION = 4;
```

So this is accepted, not rejected:

```sql
-- Accepted in 1.12. But please don't use it yet.
ALTER TABLE db.my_table SET TBLPROPERTIES ('format-version' = '4');
```

We should treat `format-version=4` in 1.12 as untested territory and leave it unset. For now, we can watch V4 become something we can begin to test against, and treat it as something wonderful that is coming in the future.

## Formal expressions spec baselined

Also contributing to the V4 scaffolding, the expressions spec was baselined and will be leveraged by future V4 features like constraints and default value expressions.

> **Take a read through the [baselined expressions specification here](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16652).**

So why is this important? Iceberg has had ad-hoc expression serialization for years. The intention of this spec is to replace the ad-hoc implementations with a real recursive grammar, as defined in [expressions-spec.md](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/main/format/expressions-spec.md).

Value expressions first:

```text
EXPR: LITERAL | REFERENCE | APPLY

REFERENCE: BOUND_REF | UNBOUND_REF
BOUND_REF:   { "type": "reference", "id": ID }
UNBOUND_REF: { "type": "reference", "name": NAME }

APPLY: { "type": "apply", "function": FUNC_REF, "arguments": [ FUNC_ARG* ] }
```

Then predicates compose them:

```text
PREDICATE: true | false
    | { "type": "not",      "child": PREDICATE }
    | { "type": BINARY_OP,  "left": PREDICATE, "right": PREDICATE }
    | { "type": UNARY_OP,   "child": EXPR }
    | { "type": CMP_OP,     "left": EXPR, "right": EXPR }
    | { "type": SET_OP,     "child": EXPR, "values": LITERALS }
    | DEPRECATED_PREDICATE

BINARY_OP: "and" | "or"
UNARY_OP:  "is-null" | "not-null" | "is-nan" | "not-nan"
CMP_OP:    "lt" | "lt-eq" | "gt" | "gt-eq" | "eq" | "not-eq"
         | "starts-with" | "not-starts-with"
SET_OP:    "in" | "not-in"
```

Why does this matter enough to call out? Server-side scan planning means shipping predicates to a catalog for push-down. Without a standard serialization, every implementation invents its own, and that is how we end up with a protocol that works only between two vendors who happened to test against each other.

The implementation detail worth remembering is the **reference**. It either serializes **by field id** or **by name**, and that encodes _when_ a column’s identity gets decided. Stored expressions like `CHECK` constraints use ids, so a rename cannot orphan them; query filters use names, resolved against the current schema on every run. The spec is explicit that _server-side planning uses unbound named references_, so the client half of scan planning sends names, not ids. Older term-based forms still parse, so clients and catalog servers can each move on their own schedule rather than having to cut over together.

> We’ll keep you posted on the expressions spec as we continue to watch the progress being made on the road to V4.

## Variant grows up

V3 gave us the Variant type. 1.11 gave us shredded writes in Spark. 1.12 is where Variant really takes center stage, and the reason is [vectorized Parquet reads](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16292).

> Note: This support is available today for unshredded Variant, with shredded support still pending as of the 1.12 release.

Before this, a single Variant column forced the _entire table_ into row-at-a-time reads. Not the column, but the entire table. If we adopted Variant in 1.11 and concluded that semi-structured data on Iceberg was slow, this is why, and the fix comes in 1.12. Arrow readers now compose over the metadata and value children with per-file shredded detection.

The best part of this change is that there is zero additional config to enable it. It is on by default for non-shredded Variant columns, with transparent fallback to row-based reads for shredded files or when the metrics mode is `none` or `counts`. No new table property or flag to flip. Just upgrade and watch the performance of Variant scans take off.

Shredding on the write side does have a knob, though, and it remains opt-in for 1.12:

```sql
ALTER TABLE db.my_table SET TBLPROPERTIES (
  'write.parquet.shred-variants' = 'true'
);
```

Around that headline sit roughly eighteen changes: [Flink can write shredded Variant](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15596), [Kafka Connect and generic Record writes](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17520) gain shredding, and a stack of allocation work — [reduced allocation in construction](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16818), [caching of adjacent identical metadata](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16852), [precomputed sorted entries](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17114). There is also [hardening against malformed Variant binary](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16568), which matters more than it sounds if we are ingesting semi-structured data from anywhere we do not fully control.

## Function endpoints arrive

Alongside it, REST catalog **function endpoints** arrive in the IRC specification:

```http
GET /v1/{prefix}/namespaces/{namespace}/functions
GET /v1/{prefix}/namespaces/{namespace}/functions/{name}
```

[Those endpoints are defined](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15180), but what ships is the OpenAPI specification and generated models. Iceberg’s own Java catalog implementations do **not** implement the function endpoints in this release.

Remote signing also becomes complete rather than half-specified. [The `remote-signing-config` object](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16822) on `LoadTableResult` is joined by [the client implementation](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17709), which also removes the legacy `s3.signer.*` properties. Signing configuration moves from our client config to whatever the catalog hands back, which is a migration item, and we will come back to it.

## Flink finally gets an answer to equality deletes

Anyone running Flink upsert at volume can understand the pain of equality deletes. Equality deletes are cheap to write and expensive to read. Every query has to join data files against delete files to work out what is actually gone. On a continuously upserting table, that compounds until read latency is dominated by delete resolution and nobody can explain to the analytics team why the dashboard got slow.

1.12 ships `ConvertEqualityDeletes`, a maintenance task that rewrites those equality deletes into deletion vectors. It landed across six pull requests — [data model and key serialization](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16831), [the reader and primary-key index](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16844), [the DV writer](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16858), [the committer](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16874), [the planner](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16889), and [the public API](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16948) — which shows the level of effort it takes to come up with a battle-hardened solution for something this delicate.

There are two ways to run it, and the choice matters more than it looks.

The explicit route wires the task into a `TableMaintenance` pipeline:

```java
TableMaintenance.forTable(env, tableLoader)
    .add(
        ConvertEqualityDeletes.builder()
            .stagingBranch("staging")
            .targetBranch("main")
            .equalityFieldColumns(ImmutableList.of("id"))
            .scheduleOnEqDeleteFileCount(10)
            .parallelism(4))
    .append();
```

Walking that through:

1. We begin by binding the maintenance pipeline to a table, handing it the Flink execution environment and a `TableLoader` (the same loader our sink already uses).
2. We then stage conversion work on a separate branch. The staging branch is where the converter accumulates its work before it lands, which keeps partially converted state away from readers on `main`.
3. We name the target branch the conversion commits to. It defaults to `SnapshotRef.MAIN_BRANCH`, so leaving it off gives us in-place conversion.
4. We declare the equality field columns. **These must match what the writer is actually using** or this operation will fail.
5. We give it a trigger. Here the task fires once ten equality delete files have accumulated; `scheduleOnCommitCount(int)` and `scheduleOnInterval(Duration)` are the alternatives.
6. Finally, we set parallelism and append the task to the pipeline.

The second route is easier because it removes step four’s failure mode entirely. [The `IcebergSink` integration](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17142) derives the equality fields from the sink’s own resolved equality field identifiers, so they _cannot_ drift out of sync with the writer:

```java
IcebergSink.forRowData(stream)
    .tableLoader(tableLoader)
    .equalityFieldColumns(ImmutableList.of("id"))
    .convertEqualityDeletes()   // equality fields derived from the sink
    .append();
```

Or, if we configure through SQL or table properties rather than code:

| Property | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `flink-maintenance.convert-equality-deletes.enabled` | Enable converting equality deletes to deletion vectors (requires equality fields and format version >= 3) | `false` |
| `flink-maintenance.convert-equality-deletes.target-branch` | Branch the converted deletion vectors are committed to | not set (in place) |
| `flink-maintenance.convert-equality-deletes.schedule.commit-count` | Trigger after N commits | `1` |
| `flink-maintenance.convert-equality-deletes.schedule.interval-second` | Trigger after a time interval, in seconds | not set |

Before we turn any of this on, the constraints deserve a careful read. There are three, and two of them are disqualifying rather than inconvenient. The table must be **format version 3 or higher**, validated at job startup. And **row lineage is not preserved** through conversion, so if we depend on `_row_id` or `_last_updated_sequence_number`, this feature is not for us yet. The third is the inconvenient one: every partition column must also be an equality field. Row lineage is the red tape I’d put in front of the team before anyone gets excited.

There is a correctness fix here worth naming, because it was open until quite recently and caused real growing pains: [deleted rows could reappear after a failed conversion cycle](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17630). Resolving an equality delete consumes index entries, and a cycle that failed _after_ resolving one never restored them, because the target branch never moved, _but the task still reported success_. Silent resurrection of deleted rows with a green task checkmark is a big reason to upgrade.

While we are in Flink, two duplicate-row bugs got fixed that have nothing to do with the new feature and everything to do with everyday upsert. In [RANGE distribution](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17276), Iceberg consulted `schema.identifierFieldIds()` instead of the equality fields we actually configured, so explicitly configured equality fields on a schema without identifier fields were simply ignored. In [HASH mode](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16243), identifier-only records were round-robined while the writer still emitted equality deletes. Both are the same underlying failure: records sharing an equality key reached different writers, so the delete never suppressed the old row and the duplicate survived. If we run Flink upsert with explicitly configured equality fields, these two are the reason to upgrade.

One more that will save somebody a very bad afternoon: [savepoint restore was impossible](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17210) for jobs using `TableMaintenance`, because the builder derived its operator ID suffix from a random UUID. Operator IDs changed on every submission, so no savepoint could ever be restored. It is now derived from the table name.

> Expect a one-time operator ID change on upgrade, and plan for it rather than discovering it.

Lastly, [reading Iceberg views from Flink SQL](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17859) arrives here too, [backported](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18104) across 2.2, 2.1, and 1.20.

## Correctness fixes and squashed bugs

Most release notes lead with features. This one shouldn’t, because 1.12 fixes a cluster of bugs that produced _silently wrong results_. Not exceptions, not failed jobs, just answers that were confidently incorrect. If you were thinking about skipping the 1.12 release, the following are really good reasons to upgrade instead.

### Deletion vector indexes

There was a bug with [deletion vector indexing](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17497) that is now resolved in 1.12. The problem was that scan planning indexes deletion vectors (DVs) by data file location alone, but a single Puffin file can hold DVs for many data files. Every DV in that file resolves to the _last_ index. So if we run DVs at any scale (and after 1.11, many of us do), this meant incorrect rows were returned, or deleted rows quietly came back to life.

### Metadata table query filtering

Adjacent to the DV bug, [metadata table queries filtering on `data_file.content`](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17440) pruned delete manifests they shouldn’t have, because a single delete manifest could store both positional and equality deletes. So even if you were auditing your tables, any tooling built to support runtime checks for your tables could also have been returning incomplete answers (depending on the table and whether it used deletes). In the same family, [negated filters on `all_manifests`](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17346) pruned every snapshot and returned zero rows even when matching delete manifests existed. The query that bit people looks completely innocent:

```sql
-- Spark parses this as Not(EqualTo), which pruned every snapshot.
-- Before 1.12 this returned zero rows even when delete manifests existed.
SELECT * FROM db.my_table.all_manifests WHERE content != 0;
```

An empty result set looks a lot like “nothing to worry about,” which is exactly the problem.

### Time travel on tables with clock skew

`SnapshotUtil` assumed the snapshot log was in chronological order. The spec makes no such promise and explicitly allows skew, so `AS OF` queries against write-audit-publish (WAP) or cherry-pick workflows could read the wrong snapshot entirely. The [fix for time travel on tables with clock skew](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17360) looks for the entry with the maximum timestamp &lt;= the requested timestamp, rather than taking the last entry’s timestamp.

### Fixed resource leaks

Resource leaks are traditionally challenging to find in large distributed systems, and they are the kind that degrade a long-running service rather than failing immediately. Both the [`HadoopCatalog` and `HiveCatalog` leaked `FileIO` on every `close()`, while the `BigQueryMetastoreCatalog` had no `close()` at all](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16862). This results in slow-motion resource exhaustion for any service that creates catalogs.

[Vectorized row-lineage reads never released their off-heap Arrow vectors](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17296), which is direct-memory exhaustion in long-running Spark and Flink scans.

If we take one thing from this section, it’s that the resource leaks alone justify this upgrade, before we look at a single feature.

### Issues that the upgrade won’t fix automatically

Let’s assume that a fixed writer can never repair what a broken writer already wrote. Mitigating that is always left to the data engineering teams, or to agents.

Three of the fixes in 1.12 correct _metrics bounds_, which are the min/max values stored in the manifest metadata that drive predicate pushdown and file skipping. Bounds are written once and persist. Upgrading corrects the code that writes them going forward. It does absolutely nothing about the bounds already sitting in our manifests. And because those bounds decide which files a query can safely skip, a wrong bound means a query silently skips a file that _does_ contain matching rows.

The specifics are narrow, and that is the good news:

- [Variant BINARY fields](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16880) with values over 16 bytes, where the stored upper bound could come out _smaller_ than a value actually in the file. Written badly by 1.9.0, 1.10.0, and 1.11.0.
- [Variant STRING fields](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17397), where bounds were merged using Java string ordering rather than UTF-8 byte order, so bounds could invert on non-BMP characters — emoji being the obvious case. Written badly by 1.10.0 and 1.11.0.
- [ORC `timestamp_ns`](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16922), where statistics were converted to microseconds while bounds serialize as nanoseconds, making bounds roughly 1000x too small. The affected version range is not stated on the pull request, and I could not determine it.

Both Variant fixes were backported to 1.9.x, 1.10.x, and 1.11.x, which tells us how seriously the community took them. Non-Variant binary and string columns were never affected, since the standard path used the right comparator.

So what do we actually do? The first step is fairly simple: find out whether we are exposed to the problem in the first place. Most teams won’t be.

```sql
-- Step 1: does this table even have an at-risk column type?
DESCRIBE TABLE db.my_table;
-- Looking for: VARIANT columns (binary or string fields inside them),
-- or TIMESTAMP_NS columns on ORC-backed tables.

-- Step 2: which Iceberg versions have written to this table?
-- Snapshot summaries carry the writer's environment context.
SELECT snapshot_id, committed_at, summary
FROM db.my_table.snapshots
ORDER BY committed_at;
```

For the second query, reading writer provenance out of snapshot summaries is an _approach_, but it isn’t a documented recipe (so there may be better ways to find this information within your setup). What keys appear in `summary` depends on what the writing engine populated, so treat this as a starting point for investigation rather than a reliable filter. If the schema check from step one comes back clean, none of this matters and we can move on with a clear conscience.

If we _are_ exposed, the remediation is to rewrite the affected files so metrics get recomputed:

```sql
-- Rewriting recomputes metrics, which replaces the bad bounds.
CALL system.rewrite_data_files(
  table => 'db.my_table',
  options => map('rewrite-all', 'true')
);
```

> Note: zero pull requests in this release propose a repair path. Not one mentions rewriting manifests, rewriting data files, or a bounds escape hatch. Rewriting the affected files is an available approach given how metrics are computed, but remember to test and validate. Until the affected files are rewritten, treat query results over those columns as untrustworthy.

For contrast, [nanosecond timestamp pushdown in Parquet](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16619), where a `timestamp_ns` predicate matched every row, is read-side only. Nothing bad actually persisted, and upgrading fully fixes it. _Remember to always think about where a bug lives: is it in code or on disk?_

## Kafka Connect

Through August, the Kafka Connect sink carried two open data-integrity issues that would have been big red flags. The first was a data-loss path that triggered on _default configuration_: a coordinator could enter a zombie state — thread alive, partitions revoked — and keep re-committing a stale control-topic offset. Nothing errored. The task looked healthy. When that offset eventually aged out of the control topic’s retention, a newly elected coordinator sought to an offset that no longer existed and, because the reset policy defaults to `latest`, skipped every record in between.

The second was duplicate file commits after task restart.

```java
// Before — an unconditional put let the tracked position move BACKWARDS
// when a control topic partition was re-read.
controlTopicOffsets.put(record.partition(), record.offset() + 1);

// After — keep the highest position ever seen.
// kafka-connect/.../connect/channel/Channel.java
controlTopicOffsets.merge(record.partition(), record.offset() + 1, Long::max);
```

That map feeds the snapshot’s `kafka.connect.offsets` watermark. Once the watermark regressed, replayed `DataWritten` envelopes passed the minimum-offset filter and the same data files got committed again — and `distinctByKey` only deduplicates within a single commit, so nothing downstream caught it. The production report behind [the fix](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17933) is worth looking at for scale: 149 double-referenced files and roughly 112,000 duplicated rows.

[The zombie-coordinator path](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17552) is closed too, by making the coordinator commit offsets only when they are greater than existing ones.

Worth knowing: the duplicate-commit fix explicitly does _not_ include the content-level backstop that was discussed — a bounded set of recently committed file locations — which was left for a follow-up. So the mechanism that caused the regression is fixed; a second, independent check against the same class of problem is not there yet.

## Upgrading to 1.12

Every consolidation release has a gotcha, and this one is mostly a deprecation purge that has been coming for a while.

### We say goodbye to Spark 3.4

Spark 3.4 is removed entirely. The `spark/v3.4` module is deleted and `iceberg-spark-runtime-3.4_2.12` will not be published. Supported versions move to 3.5.9, 4.0.4, and 4.1.3. There is no path here except upgrading Spark.

`SparkFilters` **is gone** across Spark 3.5, 4.0, and 4.1 and is replaced with `SparkV2Filters`:

```java
// Before — removed in 1.12
import org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkFilters;

// After — DSv2 Predicate[] instead of the old Filter API
import org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkV2Filters;
```

**The core removals** are the ones with the widest blast radius. Here is the migration table:

| Removed | Replacement |
| --- | --- |
| `SystemProperties` (class) | `SystemConfigs` |
| `ThreadPools.newWorkerPool(String)`, `newWorkerPool(String, int)` | `newExitingWorkerPool` for long-lived pools, `newFixedThreadPool` for short-lived |
| `SnapshotUtil.newFiles`, `newFilesBetween` | `SnapshotChanges` with `ancestorsBetween` |
| `TableScanUtil.hasDeletes(CombinedScanTask)`, `hasEqDeletes(CombinedScanTask)` | the `FileScanTask` overloads |
| `BaseScan.io()` | `table().io()` |

That `ThreadPools` split is the one most likely to be waved through in review, because the old call site still reads fine in the diff:

```java
// Before
ExecutorService pool = ThreadPools.newWorkerPool("my-pool", 8);

// After — pick based on lifetime, which is the point of the split
ExecutorService longLived  = ThreadPools.newExitingWorkerPool("my-pool", 8);
ExecutorService shortLived = ThreadPools.newFixedThreadPool("my-pool", 8);
```

### Writing position deletes with row data is no longer supported

This sounds more alarming than it is: [writes are rejected while reads are preserved](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17706), so it is not a compatibility break for existing tables. Concretely, `buildPositionWriter()` in Avro, ORC, and Parquet now throws `UnsupportedOperationException` when a row schema is set, `PositionDelete.set(CharSequence, long, R)` and the `row()` getter are removed, and Flink’s `FlinkAppenderFactory` — whose position delete path was built entirely on row data — is gone. The sharp edge is that maintenance operations encountering existing such files will now fail loudly rather than silently dropping the row column, which is the correct behavior and still a surprise if we hit it during a rewrite at 2 a.m.

### S3 remote signing

If we configure S3 remote signing, the `s3.signer.*` properties are removed and that configuration moves server-side, per the `remote-signing-config` work above.

### Performance improvements to Hive catalog table listings

That covers the breaking changes. On to the improvements, starting with a genuinely useful one: [Hive catalog table listing](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17317) no longer loads every table object into client memory. The old path timed out at roughly 46,000 tables even with a 900-second socket timeout. The same namespace now lists in about five seconds. If we run a large Hive Metastore, that is the number to bring to the upgrade conversation.

### Fix for unbounded row groups

Most of the performance work in 1.12 is opt-in, which means we get none of it by default. This one is worth opting into.

```sql
-- Enforce the row-group target against uncompressed size. Without this,
-- GZIP/ZSTD tables compare compressed bytes to an uncompressed target
-- and row groups grow unbounded.
ALTER TABLE db.my_table SET TBLPROPERTIES (
  'write.parquet.row-group-size-track-uncompressed' = 'true'
);
```

### Performance improvements for small-file and metadata-heavy workloads

For Parquet-based tables, the read path gets a huge improvement for free. Opening a Parquet file normally means several round trips: one for the footer length, one for the footer body, then one per row group. `EagerInputFile` collapses all those calls into a single fetch, and [it is now wired into the Parquet read path](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17284). This is especially important for small-file and metadata-heavy workloads, since compaction, manifest reads, scan planning, and streaming polls all pay that footer latency linearly in file count.

> This integration lives in the `parquet` module rather than in any engine tree, so **it is not a Spark thing or a Flink thing** — every engine reading Parquet through Iceberg gets it. There is also no property to tune. The threshold is a private constant:
>
> ```java
> // From parquet/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/parquet/Parquet.java
> private static final long EAGER_FETCH_THRESHOLD_BYTES = 1024 * 1024;   // 1 MB
>
> private static boolean canEagerFetch(long fileLength) {
>   return fileLength > 0 && fileLength <= EAGER_FETCH_THRESHOLD_BYTES;
> }
> ```
>
> So files at or below 1 MB are fetched eagerly and everything larger behaves as before. We do not opt in, and (at this point) we cannot tune it upward for a workload that might benefit from a larger window.

### Opting into Hilbert-curve clustering

Compaction gets a new option. [Hilbert-curve clustering](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16827) joins Z-order, preserving locality more consistently for multidimensional data (where points close together in space stay close along the curve, without the large jumps Z-order produces at certain boundaries):

```sql
CALL system.rewrite_data_files(
  table => 'db.tbl',
  strategy => 'sort',
  sort_order => 'hilbert(c1, c2)'
);
```

Because it is expressed as a sort order rather than a new strategy, adopting it is a one-line change to an existing rewrite rather than a new maintenance job.

### Flink version support changes

The `flink/v2.0` module is gone now, with **2.2 and 2.3 support added**. The matrix is now 1.20, 2.1, 2.2, and 2.3. If you were on 2.0, upgrading will make supporting equality deletes so much easier.

## Where that leaves us

1.12 is a consolidation release paving the way for V4. The V4 commits are numerous, visible, and not yet usable. The release is concentrated in four places: a cluster of correctness repairs, a real solution to Flink equality deletes, Variant becoming fast, and the arrival of a formal expressions specification that the REST catalog ecosystem is going to lean on for years.

As a side note, before we upgrade, one checklist item that nothing else will catch for us: if we have Variant binary or string columns, or ORC `timestamp_ns` columns, written by 1.9 through 1.11, those bounds are already wrong on disk and the upgrade will not repair them. A fixed writer never repairs what a broken writer already wrote.

---

Thanks to all the [Apache Iceberg contributors](https://iceberg.apache.org/releases/#1120-release) who helped make this release a success. Also, a shout-out to [Jason Reid](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jasonreid/), [Daniel Weeks](https://www.linkedin.com/in/daniel-weeks-a1946860/), and [Anoop Johnson](https://www.linkedin.com/in/anoopjohnson/) from [Databricks](https://www.linkedin.com/company/databricks/posts/?feedView=all), and to [Neelesh Salian](https://www.linkedin.com/in/neeleshsalian/), who all helped with the technical review of this post, and a special thanks to Neelesh, who was the release manager for 1.12.

---

*This post was originally published by Scott Haines as
[“A Field Guide to Apache Iceberg 1.12”](https://datacircus.substack.com/p/a-field-guide-to-apache-iceberg-112)
on [Distributed Thoughts](https://datacircus.substack.com/). Republished here with attribution to the original
source.*

# Apache Iceberg 1.11.0 Release

URL: https://iceberg.apache.org/blog/apache-iceberg-1.11.0-release/
Republished at: https://openlakehouse.io/blog/iceberg/iceberg-1-11-0-release
Original publisher: Apache Iceberg
Date: 2026-06-16
Category: Iceberg

The Apache Iceberg community is pleased to announce the release of Apache Iceberg 1.11.0. This release is the result of over **1,000 commits** from **200+ contributors**. See the [release notes](https://iceberg.apache.org/releases/#1110-release) for the complete list of changes.

## Release Highlights

### REST Catalog: A More Complete Protocol

1.11.0 represents the most significant step forward for the REST catalog protocol since it was introduced.

[Remote scan planning](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/13400) allows catalog servers to plan table scans and stream back file scan tasks directly. Previously, every client had to fetch manifest lists and manifests itself to determine which files to read. With server-side planning, clients receive only the relevant scan tasks, reducing driver memory pressure and enabling server-side optimizations that are transparent to the query engine. This release extends remote scan planning to cover [incremental scans](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14661) for Structured Streaming workloads and [metadata tables](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14881) such as `history` and `snapshots`. A [per-table override](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15572) allows individual tables to opt out of catalog-level scan planning mode when needed.

[Freshness-aware table loading](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14398) adds ETag-based caching to table metadata. When a client loads a table it already has metadata for, the server can return a `304 Not Modified` response instead of re-sending the full metadata payload, cutting unnecessary round-trips in tight read loops and interactive workloads.

[Idempotency key support](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14740) introduces a standard `Idempotency-Key` header for mutating catalog operations. Retried writes — commits, creates, and drops — are now guaranteed not to execute twice, preventing duplicate snapshots and corrupted state from network timeouts.

[Register View](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14868) completes the view lifecycle in the REST catalog. Just as tables can be registered from their metadata location, views can now be [registered via the REST API](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14870) too — enabling cross-catalog migrations and re-attaching orphaned view metadata.

[Custom Table and View Operations](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14465) can now be injected into the REST catalog, allowing users to extend or override default `TableOperations` and `ViewOperations` behavior without forking the catalog implementation.

### OpenAPI Specification Updates

Several protocol-level additions land in the OpenAPI spec this release, tightening the contract between clients and catalog servers.

- **Namespace separator configurable by server**: [The server can now advertise a custom namespace separator](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14448) in the config endpoint, allowing catalogs that use separators other than `.` to communicate this to clients without out-of-band configuration.
- **Register view endpoint**: [A new `/register-view` REST endpoint](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14869) is added to the OpenAPI spec, enabling view registration as an independently authorized catalog capability.
- **ETag for `CommitTableResponse`**: [ETag support on commit responses](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14760) enables clients to detect whether a concurrent write changed the table between their load and commit.
- **S3 signing endpoint promoted to main spec**: [The S3 signing endpoint](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15450) moves from an extension into the main OpenAPI spec, making it an official part of the REST catalog protocol.
- **Partition statistics in `TableUpdate`**: [`SetPartitionStatisticsUpdate` and `RemovePartitionStatisticsUpdate`](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14957) are now included in the `TableUpdate` union type.
- **Storage credentials in scan planning responses**: [Storage credentials are now returned](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15524) in `PlanTableScanResponse` and `FetchPlanningResultResponse` when the `include-credentials` flag is set.

### Spec: SQL UDFs and Geospatial Types

The [SQL UDF Specification](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14117) introduces a new spec for storing SQL user-defined functions in Iceberg catalogs. UDFs are versioned, support multiple SQL dialects, and are portable across engines, bringing function management into the catalog layer for the first time.

[Geospatial bounding box types](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/12667) add native bounding box types and an `INTERSECTS` predicate to Iceberg's type system, enabling spatial partition pruning and file skipping for geospatial workloads directly on Iceberg tables. [Restrictions for geometry types in V3](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14250) are also clarified in this release.

Several smaller but meaningful spec additions round out the release:

- **`added-rows` in snapshot fields**: The [`added-rows` field is restored to snapshot metadata](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14048).
- **`referenced-by` in `loadTable` response**: [`loadTable` now returns a `referenced-by` field](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/13810) listing views and other objects that depend on the table.
- **`scan-planning-mode` in `LoadTableResult`**: [The server can now advertise its preferred scan planning mode](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14867).
- **404 for missing warehouse on config endpoint**: [The `/v1/config` endpoint now returns 404](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15746) when the requested warehouse does not exist.

### Performance and Reliability

[LIMIT pushdown to scan](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14615) stops scanning after enough rows are found when a query includes a `LIMIT` clause, rather than reading all matching files. For exploratory queries, this can reduce I/O by orders of magnitude.

Vectorized reads now cover additional Parquet encodings, eliminating the row-at-a-time fallback for [BYTE_STREAM_SPLIT](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15373), [DELTA_LENGTH_BYTE_ARRAY, and DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15362).

[Snapshot expiration cleanup modes](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14287) introduce a new `cleanupMode` API that gives finer control over what gets cleaned up when snapshots expire.

[Unique table locations](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/12892) via a new catalog property append a UUID to table storage paths, preventing a data loss scenario where `DeleteOrphanFiles` could remove files from a renamed table.

Scheduled credential refresh for [AWS S3FileIO](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15678) and [GCS FileIO](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15696) proactively rotates credentials before they expire, eliminating transient failures in long-running Spark and Flink jobs.

The [GCSAnalyticsCore library](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14333) is now integrated into GCSFileIO, bringing analytics-optimized I/O for Google Cloud Storage.

### Format V4 Foundations

1.11.0 begins laying the groundwork for Table Format V4.

New foundational types — [TrackedFile, TrackingInfo, ContentInfo, and ManifestStats](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15049) — are the building blocks for V4's adaptive metadata tree.

The new [FormatModel abstraction](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/12774) replaces hardcoded file format handling with a pluggable interface. [Parquet](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15253), [ORC](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15255), Avro, and Arrow each now implement a `FormatModel` contract.

### Encryption

1.11.0 makes table encryption available to Iceberg users. The [Encryption integration and test](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/13066) activates the encryption mechanism in Hive tables via a table property containing the ID of the table master key.

[Manifest list encryption](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/7770) extends Iceberg's encryption coverage to manifest list files. [Automatic key rotation](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14396) adds support for rotating key encryption keys without manual intervention.

[Cloud KMS support](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15272) now covers AWS, Azure, and GCP through a unified `encryption.kms-type` property.

### New APIs

The [Content Stats API](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/13933) introduces classes for file-level statistics — min/max values, null counts, and more — providing richer information for query planners.

The [Partition Stats Scan API](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14640) replaces the old single-shot partition stats reader with a composable, filterable interface consistent with the rest of Iceberg's Scan API.

### Engine Updates

#### Spark

[Spark 4.1](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14155) is now supported, with several notable additions:

- **MERGE INTO schema evolution**: [Initial support](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14970) for schema changes during merge writes
- **Shredded Variant writes**: [Support for writing shredded Variant data](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14297) in Iceberg-Spark
- **Async micro-batch planner**: [Reduces scheduling overhead](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15299) in Structured Streaming
- **Adaptive split sizing**: [Session config support](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16088) for tuning split sizes and parallelism

**[Spark 3.4 support is deprecated](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14099)** in this release.

#### Flink

[Flink 2.1](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/13714) is now supported and Flink 1.19 has been removed.

**Row lineage** readers for [`_row_id` and `_last_updated_sequence_number`](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14148) are now available in Flink, with [row lineage preserved through RewriteDataFiles](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14149).

The Flink Dynamic Sink receives major improvements:

- **Deletion vector support**: [Efficient row-level deletes](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14414) without rewriting data files
- **Variant type support**: [Variant is now supported in Flink 2.1](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15265)
- **Schema evolution**: [Support for dropping columns](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14728) and [case-insensitive field matching](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14729)
- **SQL-configurable options**: Dynamic Sink options are now configurable through [Flink SQL](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15279)
- **Post-commit maintenance**: [Arbitrary maintenance tasks can now be registered via the IcebergSink Builder](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15566)

[Nanosecond timestamp precision](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15475) is now supported, matching the full range of Iceberg's timestamp spec.

#### Kafka Connect

- **Variant type ingestion**: [Semi-structured JSON data](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15283) can now be ingested directly into Iceberg's Variant type
- **Table UUID validation on commit**: [Verifies table identity at commit time](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14979)
- **SMT offset tracking fix**: [Fixes a bug](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15880) where Single Message Transforms could cause duplicate records

### Cloud Integrations

**AWS**: The [KMS endpoint is now configurable](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14246), [chunked encoding for S3 requests is configurable](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15242), custom credential providers are [preferred over the default chain](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15249), and [retry policies now apply to Glue and DynamoDB clients](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15094).

**Azure**: A [KeyManagementClient implementation for Azure Key Vault](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/13186) adds native Azure KMS support, and [token credential provider support](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14136) enables flexible authentication including managed identity and service principal flows.

**GCP**: [Service account impersonation in BigQueryMetastoreCatalog](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14447), a new [`gcp.auth.credentials-key` property](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14713) for base64-encoded service account keys, and [ETag-based conflict detection on commit](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14940).

**Aliyun**: [RRSA authentication is now supported for OSS](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14443).

## Breaking Changes

- **Apache DataFusion Comet removed**: [The Comet integration has been removed](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15674) from the Spark module
- **Java 11 dropped**: [Java 11 support has been removed](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14400); Java 17 is now the minimum required version
- **Flink 1.19 removed**: [Flink 1.19 support has been removed](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/13714); upgrade to Flink 1.20 or 2.x

## Dependency Updates

Notable version changes in this release:

- **AWS SDK**: 2.33.0 → 2.44.4
- **Parquet**: 1.16.0 → 1.17.1
- **ORC**: 1.9.7 → 1.9.8
- **Avro**: 1.12.0 → 1.12.1
- **Nessie**: 0.104.5 → 0.107.5
- **Guava**: 33.4.8-jre → 33.6.0-jre
- **Hadoop**: 3.4.1 → 3.4.3
- **Jetty**: 11.0.26 → 12.1.8

New support added for Spark 4.1 (4.1.1) and Flink 2.1 (2.1.0).

## Getting Involved

Apache Iceberg is developed by a community of contributors. We use GitHub [issues](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/issues) for tracking work and the [Apache Iceberg Community Slack](https://iceberg.apache.org/community/#slack) for discussions.

The easiest way to get started is to:

1. Try Apache Iceberg with your workloads and report any issues you encounter
2. Review the [contributor guide](https://iceberg.apache.org/contribute/)
3. Look for [good first issues](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/contribute)

For more information, visit the [Apache Iceberg repository](https://github.com/apache/iceberg) or the [documentation](https://iceberg.apache.org/docs/latest/).

[“Apache Iceberg 1.11.0 Release”](https://iceberg.apache.org/blog/apache-iceberg-1.11.0-release/)
on the Apache Iceberg blog. Republished here with attribution to the original
source.*

# Integrating the Rust Delta Kernel into ClickHouse

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/blog/delta-lake/clickhouse-delta-kernel
Date: 2026-05-18
Category: Delta Lake

Unless you've spent the last few years in a cave without internet access,
you've probably heard of open table formats like Delta Lake and Iceberg.

The goal is simple: define a data format that any query engine can read and
write, as long as it follows the protocol. Over time, these formats have
evolved beyond simple interoperability, introducing richer table semantics
such as transactional support, schema evolution, and versioned data
management directly on top of the underlying data.

Recently, we announced that [ClickHouse is data lake ready](https://clickhouse.com/blog/clickhouse-is-data-lake-ready),
with it supporting these table formats as a query engine. As part of that
journey, we've been working more closely with these formats and, like many
others, have run into some of the same challenges.

Adopting these table formats is not trivial. Supporting them requires keeping
up with complex and evolving protocols, whether through external libraries or
custom implementations. Each query engine remains responsible for maintaining
its own integration, often leading to fragmented feature support and
increasing maintenance overhead.

In this post, we explore how we addressed this by integrating the Rust Delta
Kernel into ClickHouse. This provides a maintained and consistent interface
between the table format and ClickHouse's query engine, enabling us to expose
more features while significantly reducing integration complexity.

## What is ClickHouse?

ClickHouse is a high-performance, column-oriented SQL database management
system (DBMS) for online analytical processing (OLAP). OLAP refers to SQL
queries with complex calculations (e.g., aggregations, string processing,
arithmetic) over massive datasets, processing billions and trillions of rows
in milliseconds.

For an introduction to ClickHouse, including why it exists and how it
delivers its performance, we recommend the
[Getting Started Guides](https://clickhouse.com/docs/get-started/quick-start).
For a deeper look at the architectural decisions behind its speed, see the
["Why ClickHouse is Fast"](https://clickhouse.com/docs/concepts/why-clickhouse-is-so-fast) series.

For the rest of this post, we'll focus specifically on ClickHouse's
integration with Delta Lake, exploring how we integrated with the Delta
Kernel.

## Working with Delta Lake

One of the key goals in making ClickHouse data lake ready was enabling users
to query data directly from open table formats like Delta Lake. Our initial
approach involved implementing native support by working directly with the
[Delta protocol](https://github.com/delta-io/delta/blob/master/PROTOCOL.md).
While this gave us full control, it also exposed the complexity of the format
and the ongoing cost of keeping up with an evolving specification.

```sql
SELECT
    cityHash64(URL),
    count() AS cnt
FROM deltaLake('https://datasets-documentation.s3.amazonaws.com/lake_formats/delta_lake/')
GROUP BY cityHash64(URL)
ORDER BY cnt DESC
LIMIT 5
```

Results in the following:

```
   ┌──────cityHash64(URL)─┬─────cnt─┐
1. │  8128408125044552281 │ 3288173 │
2. │ 17146718649009901992 │ 1625250 │
3. │   935030221159485792 │  791465 │
4. │  6972355099133249997 │  582400 │
5. │ 13961208022208327194 │  514984 │
   └──────────────────────┴─────────┘

5 rows in set. Elapsed: 3.878 sec. Processed 100.00 million rows, 14.82 GB.
```

As support expanded, it became clear that achieving full feature coverage
while keeping the integration maintainable would be increasingly difficult.
This led us to adopt the Delta Kernel, allowing us to offload protocol
handling and focus on what ClickHouse does best: high-performance query
execution.

## Introducing the Delta Kernel

The Delta Lake kernel abstracts away much of the complexity of the underlying
format, providing a clear boundary between the query engine and the protocol.
It handles the processing of Delta files and exposes well-defined interfaces
to the engine, allowing ClickHouse to operate on "black box" objects without
managing the underlying mechanics.

In contrast to our original approach, where ClickHouse directly implemented
the protocol, this reduces both implementation complexity and maintenance
overhead while making it easier to keep pace with new features.

The Delta Kernel provides a set of guarantees that make it an attractive
foundation for supporting Delta Lake, without requiring the engine to
implement the protocol itself. In particular, it takes responsibility for:

- Parsing transaction logs stored as JSON
- Reading and interpreting Delta metadata
- Resolving snapshots and determining the correct set of data files
- Applying data skipping based on metadata

By centralizing this logic, the Kernel removes the need for each query
engine to independently implement and maintain support for an evolving
protocol.

At the same time, query engines like ClickHouse still need to retain control
over performance-critical components, particularly file reading. Significant
engineering effort goes into optimizing Parquet readers, and these
optimizations are essential to overall query performance.

The Delta Kernel is designed with this balance in mind. Through its Engine
APIs, it allows engines to plug in their own optimized implementations for
components such as file access and data reading, providing metadata about
data files including statistics and deletion vectors to allow ClickHouse to
do efficient downstream filtering and processing. It also informs the query
engine of any transformations that need to be applied to the on-disk data to
make it match the table's logical format, in addition to higher-level
interfaces for interacting with snapshots.

## What the Delta Kernel adds

Beyond abstracting the complexity of the Delta protocol, the Delta Kernel
unlocks a number of capabilities that would have been more challenging to
implement and maintain ourselves. Instead of building and evolving support
for each feature independently, we inherit a consistent and well-defined
implementation that allows us to expose these features directly in
ClickHouse.

### Writes

The Delta Kernel provides full support for managing writes to Delta tables
at the transactional level, including handling transaction logs and ensuring
consistency. Delta Lake guarantees ACID semantics for these operations,
preventing partial or conflicting updates and enabling safe concurrent
access patterns that are difficult to implement correctly from scratch. The
underlying Parquet data files are written by ClickHouse, while the Delta
Kernel is responsible solely for coordinating and recording the associated
transactional metadata.

### Schema evolution

Delta tables can evolve over time without requiring full rewrites. Columns
can be added or modified in a controlled way, with all changes tracked in
the transaction log. This allows ClickHouse to interact with datasets whose
structure changes over time without breaking queries or pipelines.

To achieve this, the Delta Kernel exposes both the logical schema, which
reflects how the table is presented to users, and the physical schema used
by the underlying Parquet files. For each data file, it also provides schema
transformation metadata, enabling ClickHouse to reconcile differences
between file-level schemas and the current table definition.

### Time travel

Every change to a Delta table is versioned, allowing queries against
previous snapshots of the data. This enables reproducibility, auditing, and
debugging workflows, as users can query historical versions of a dataset
without maintaining separate copies.

The Delta Kernel supports flexible, versioned access patterns, allowing
users to read a table at a specific snapshot. It also provides row-level
change visibility through Change Data Feed (CDF), exposing inserts, updates,
and deletes as a stream of events. In ClickHouse 25.12, we
[exposed Delta Lake's CDF](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/90431)
through the [`deltaLake` table function](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/table-functions/deltalake),
allowing users to query row-level changes between table versions:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM deltaLake('s3://path/to/table')
SETTINGS
    delta_lake_snapshot_start_version = 5,
    delta_lake_snapshot_end_version = 10;
```

Results include metadata columns such as `_change_type`, `_commit_version`,
and `_commit_timestamp`, allowing users to reason about how data has
evolved over time.

### Partition pruning

Delta metadata includes partition information that allows engines to skip
entire subsets of data during query execution. By exposing this through the
Kernel, ClickHouse can avoid scanning irrelevant files and reduce I/O,
improving query performance.

### Statistics-based pruning

In addition to partitions, Delta tracks file-level statistics such as min
and max values. These can be used for data skipping, allowing queries to
ignore files that cannot satisfy a given predicate. This is a key
optimization for large datasets, significantly reducing the amount of data
that needs to be read.

## Using the Delta Kernel in ClickHouse: a Rust library in a C++ database

To see how this integration fits into ClickHouse, it's important to first
understand the design of its build system.

### The ClickHouse build system

The resulting binary has no external dependencies, with the sole exception
of libc. The default Linux build depends only on a relatively old glibc
version — 2.4 for x86\_64 (nearly 20 years old) or 2.18 (around 11 years
old) for ARM. It does not rely on libstdc++ or any other external libraries.

Since dynamic loading is not possible, all dependencies must be built into
the binary. We vendor them as submodules within the repository under
`contrib/`. External dependencies are built using the same compiler options
and flags as the core codebase, and we maintain our own simplified CMake
configurations for each dependency.

### Rust inside ClickHouse

Rust [was introduced to ClickHouse](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/33435)
as a way to add minor functionality. The initial demonstration introduced
the [BLAKE3](https://github.com/BLAKE3-team/BLAKE3) crate using hand-written
C wrappers and [Corrosion](https://github.com/corrosion-rs/corrosion) to
handle the `cmake` targets. Other libraries followed, including
[prql](https://github.com/PRQL/prql), [skim](https://github.com/skim-rs/skim),
and ClickHouse's own
[chcache](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/tree/4baea3af01456dfd4c64c87f07657836c55014e7/rust/chcache).

To meet ClickHouse's sanitizer requirements (ASAN, MSAN, TSAN, UBSAN), we
needed Rust's sanitizer support, which depends on unstable features only
available on nightly. To eliminate flaky network failures during builds, we
[vendored all crates](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/62297)
using [cargo-local-registry](https://github.com/dhovart/cargo-local-registry)
and disabled online fetching.

### Integrating delta-kernel-rs

[delta-kernel-rs](https://github.com/delta-io/delta-kernel-rs/) did not fit
the previous "copy sources into the build directory" approach. The crate we
care about (`ffi`) uses path-based links to parent directories and
references other crates within the same repository. Copying sources breaks
those assumptions.

Instead, we now build the project in place, preserving its original
workspace structure. We generate a single `Cargo.toml` per build
configuration and pass it via
[Cargo's `--config` flag](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/d05a951295ed8e86187c421ca2c912b872de77e6/contrib/delta-kernel-rs-cmake/CMakeLists.txt#L78-L95).
To avoid cross-workspace cache conflicts, we
[fixed Corrosion](https://github.com/corrosion-rs/corrosion/pull/609) to
isolate build artifacts per workspace or configuration.

#### OpenSSL dependency

Deep in its dependency graph, `delta-kernel-rs` pulls in the
[`openssl` crate](https://crates.io/crates/openssl), which links against the
system-installed OpenSSL dynamic library — conflicting with our no-system-
dependencies rule. After iterating on Cargo flags, we configured this
through Corrosion to link against our own
[statically built OpenSSL library](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/d05a951295ed8e86187c421ca2c912b872de77e6/contrib/delta-kernel-rs-cmake/CMakeLists.txt#L71-L76).

#### Broken cross-compilation

After integration, cross-compilation was failing because Cargo was
attempting to
[build dynamic libraries](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/76807)
that referenced system libraries unavailable in the target environment. The
fix was to restrict the build to `staticlib` only. In the process, we
uncovered [a Cargo bug](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/15312),
now fixed, where specifying `--crate-type=staticlib` multiple times broke
incremental builds.

#### Random CI failures due to missing sanitizer symbols

After integration, we began seeing inexplicable linker errors about missing
[ASAN symbols](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/76921#issuecomment-2688688637)
in non-sanitizer builds. We traced the issue to sccache; upgrading from
0.7.7 to 0.10.0 initially appeared to resolve it, but the problem
resurfaced and we have since disabled sccache for Rust builds.

## Contributing back to the ecosystem

Operating at ClickHouse-scale surfaces edge cases and performance
bottlenecks that rarely appear in smaller environments. Rather than
maintaining long-lived forks, we have prioritized contributing improvements
upstream:

- **[Improved logging flexibility for debugging performance issues](https://github.com/delta-io/delta-kernel-rs/pull/1111)**:
  enabling logging to be configured dynamically at runtime, improving
  operational introspection for tables with large numbers of metadata files.

- **[Asynchronous metadata processing for improved scalability](https://github.com/delta-io/delta-kernel-rs/pull/1827)**:
  modifying the FFI interface to pass handles instead of references, so
  metadata operations (including object storage reads) can be parallelized
  outside a single-threaded callback.

## Looking forward

One immediate limitation is the inability to create empty Delta Lake tables
through the Rust kernel. Today, ClickHouse can attach to existing Delta
tables and infer their schema:

```sql
CREATE TABLE hits_delta
    ENGINE = DeltaLake('https://datasets-documentation.s3.amazonaws.com/lake_formats/delta_lake/')
```

But it cannot initialize a new table and materialize the corresponding
Delta log and metadata on object storage. Addressing this would let users
define tables directly from ClickHouse backed by Delta Lake from the outset.

The Change Data Feed (CDF) support described earlier will also provide the
foundation for CDC-oriented workflows on top of Delta Lake data in
ClickPipes. Exposing table history, commit timelines, and version metadata
as native system tables in ClickHouse would make it significantly easier to
understand data evolution and operate incremental workloads.

## Conclusion

Integrating the Rust Delta Kernel into ClickHouse represents a shift in how
we approach open table formats, moving from bespoke implementations toward
shared, well-defined abstractions. This has allowed us to accelerate feature
development, reduce maintenance overhead, and focus on delivering
high-performance analytics at scale. By contributing improvements upstream
and continuing to close the remaining gaps, we hope to shape a more robust
and interoperable data lake ecosystem.

---

*This post was originally published on the
[Delta Lake blog](https://delta.io/blog/2026-05-18-integrating-the-rust-delta-kernel-into-clickhouse/)
by Melvyn Peignon, Kseniia Sumarokova, and Raul Marin. Republished here with
attribution to the original authors.*
