# One catalog, many engines: Unity Catalog OSS with Spark, DuckDB, PyIceberg and Trino on Delta and Iceberg

> Write once, read from whatever engine fits the question.

A multi-engine catalog architecture puts an open catalog between the tables and every engine that uses them. Unity Catalog OSS stores table metadata in Postgres, exposes Delta tables through its own API and Iceberg tables through the Iceberg REST catalog specification, and vends short-lived storage credentials per table. Apache Spark, DuckDB, PyIceberg and Trino then read and write the same data without copies, and access is decided once, in the catalog.

## When to use it
- Different teams prefer different engines for the same data.
- You want to stop copying data into a warehouse per tool.
- You want storage credentials vended per table instead of shared keys.

## When not to
- Expecting identical feature support in every engine: write support differs by engine, format and catalog version.

## Components

| Capability | Component | Role | Version |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source systems | Pipelines and notebooks | Create and update tables |  |
| Batch and SQL | Apache Spark | Delta notebooks on Spark 4.2.0; Iceberg notebooks on Spark 4.1.3 | 4.2.0 / 4.1.3 |
| Other engines | PyIceberg | JVM-free Iceberg reads and writes |  |
| Other engines | DuckDB | Attaches the Iceberg REST endpoint for SQL reads |  |
| Other engines | Trino | Distributed SQL over the same catalog |  |
| Catalog and credentials | Unity Catalog OSS | Delta API, Iceberg REST catalog and credential vending | 0.7.0 |
| Catalog and credentials | PostgreSQL | Catalog metadata | 16.3 |
| Open table format | Delta Lake | Catalog-managed Delta tables |  |
| Open table format | Apache Iceberg | Native Iceberg tables through Iceberg REST |  |
| Object storage | RustFS | S3-compatible storage with STS credentials | 1.0.0 |
| Dashboards and notebooks | marimo | Reactive notebooks on :2718 and :2719 |  |

## How data flows
1. **Create through the catalog.** A Spark session configured with the Unity Catalog connector creates a managed Delta table, or an Iceberg table through the Iceberg REST endpoint.
2. **Catalog records metadata.** Unity Catalog stores the table, its location and its format in Postgres.
3. **Credentials are vended.** When an engine loads a table, the catalog returns short-lived storage credentials scoped to that table's path.
4. **Another engine reads.** DuckDB or PyIceberg connects to the same Iceberg REST endpoint and reads the table directly from object storage.

## Run it

### [open-lakehouse/unitycatalog-playground](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/unitycatalog-playground)

Unity Catalog OSS on your machine with Spark, Delta and Iceberg in marimo notebooks, Postgres for metadata and RustFS for storage.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/open-lakehouse/unitycatalog-playground.git
cd unitycatalog-playground
just uc=local start
```

### [open-lakehouse/unitycatalog-rs](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/unitycatalog-rs)

A Rust implementation of the same catalog APIs, useful when you want a single binary or Helm chart.

```bash
pip install 'unitycatalog-rs[all]'   # the Python client, the uc CLI, the server and the web UI
uc dev                               # a server on http://localhost:8080, with the web UI
uc catalog list                      # upstream's bin/uc commands
```

### [open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass)

Chapter 11 has DuckDB read the Spark-written Iceberg tables through Unity Catalog 0.7's Iceberg REST endpoint.

## Caveats
- iceberg-spark-runtime exists only for Spark 4.0 and 4.1 at the time of writing, which is why the playground's Iceberg notebook runs Spark 4.1.3.
- The RustFS STS credential in the playground expires after 12 hours; refresh it with just uc=local rotate-creds.
- The playground needs at least 4 GB of Docker memory and is not for production.

## Industry use cases
- **Telecommunications: Network planning on many engines.** Run heavy jobs in Spark and interactive exploration in Trino against one catalog.
- **Cybersecurity: Threat hunting with any engine.** Hunt in DuckDB or Trino over the same tables that Spark writes.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is an Iceberg REST catalog?

An HTTP API defined by the Apache Iceberg project for creating, loading and committing Iceberg tables. Any engine that speaks it can use any catalog that implements it, including Unity Catalog OSS, Apache Polaris and Lakekeeper.

### Can Spark and DuckDB share the same tables?

Yes. Point both at the same catalog: Spark through the Unity Catalog connector or Iceberg REST, DuckDB through its Iceberg extension attached to the Iceberg REST endpoint.

### What is credential vending?

The catalog hands an engine short-lived storage credentials scoped to one table's location when the engine loads it, so engines never hold long-lived bucket keys.

## Sources
- [unitycatalog-playground README](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/unitycatalog-playground#readme)
- [Iceberg REST catalog spec](https://iceberg.apache.org/rest-catalog-spec/)
- [Unity Catalog OSS](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog)

Last updated: 2026-11-21. Canonical page: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/multi-engine-catalog

---

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/governed-ai-agents

# Governed AI agents for data engineering: Spark Declarative Pipelines, Spark Connect, Kubernetes and a governed Iceberg REST catalog

> Agents write pipeline specs; the platform decides what they are allowed to touch.

Governed AI data engineering is an architecture in which AI agents author data pipelines but never hold direct power over data. The agent writes declarative Spark Declarative Pipelines specs as a pull request; CI dry-runs them against the real catalog; a controller applies approved changes. Each tenant reaches Spark only through one identity-pinned Spark Connect ingress behind mTLS, executors run as Kubernetes pods, and a governed Iceberg REST catalog authorizes every request and vends storage credentials scoped to that tenant. Each layer owns one job, so a mistake in one does not become a breach in another.

## When to use it
- You want AI agents to build or change pipelines without giving them production credentials.
- You need per-tenant isolation on shared Spark infrastructure.
- You want defects caught before any data is processed.

## When not to
- A single-user sandbox: the masterclass's local agent chapter is the lighter starting point.

## Components

| Capability | Component | Role | Version |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source systems | AI coding agent | Writes inert pipeline specs as a pull request |  |
| Agent harness and policy | Omnigent | Agent harness with tools and policies |  |
| Models and gateway | Ollama | Local model for the course's agent chapter |  |
| Spark Connect sessions | Spark Connect | The single identity-pinned ingress per tenant | 4.1.2 |
| Batch and SQL | Apache Spark | Executors do the work | 4.1.2 |
| Declarative pipelines | Spark Declarative Pipelines | Declarative authoring: specs, not imperative jobs | Spark 4.1.2 |
| Catalog and credentials | Lakekeeper | Governed Iceberg REST catalog with per-principal authorization and credential vending | 0.13.1 |
| Open table format | Apache Iceberg | Tables under per-tenant prefixes | 1.11.0 |
| Object storage | Amazon S3 | Data under per-tenant prefixes with STS-scoped credentials |  |
| Access control and policy | Envoy | mTLS on :15009; routes each client certificate to its tenant | 1.31.5 |
| Access control and policy | OpenFGA | Authorization model behind the catalog | 1.14.0 |
| Runtime, CI/CD and IaC | GitOps CI gate | PR-only output, dry run against the real catalog, reconcile |  |
| Runtime, CI/CD and IaC | Kubernetes | Client-mode driver plus executor pods on EKS | EKS 1.31 |

## How data flows
1. **Agent proposes.** The agent writes Spark Declarative Pipelines specs and opens a pull request; it has no direct write path.
2. **CI dry-runs.** CI runs the pipeline in dry-run mode against the real catalog, catching structural defects before any data is processed.
3. **Identity-pinned ingress.** The tenant's client certificate reaches Envoy, which routes by its SPIFFE URI SAN to that tenant's Spark Connect server.
4. **Executors run.** Kubernetes schedules executor pods that do the work.
5. **Catalog authorizes.** Lakekeeper with OpenFGA authorizes each table operation and vends STS credentials scoped to the tenant's prefix.

## Run it

### [open-lakehouse/safe-spark-agents-paper](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/safe-spark-agents-paper)

Working paper, reproducible study and open reference architecture for safe, governed AI data engineering on Apache Spark.

```bash
cd study
python3 analysis/analyze.py results/results.powered.AB.n12.final.jsonl --tasks config/TASKS.lock.json --assume-backend local
```

### [open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass)

Chapter 3 runs an agent on Omnigent with a local Ollama model, MCP tools and ALLOW, DENY and ASK policies; chapter 13 has a coding agent operate the stack through AGENTS.md.

### [open-lakehouse/lakehouse-agent-kit](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/lakehouse-agent-kit)

Early-stage agent skills for the open lakehouse, driven by a connection profile instead of hardcoded hosts (lakehouse-core ships today).

## Caveats
- The isolation proof runs on one Spark Connect server per tenant; a shared-server design is described as frontier work in the paper.
- The five isolation links are proven one at a time, not as one composed request.
- Unity Catalog OSS 0.5.0, evaluated as an alternate catalog, could not do per-principal authorization on its Iceberg REST path.

## Industry use cases
- **Payments and fintech: Governed agent for merchant support.** Let an agent answer settlement questions with tools limited by policy.
- **Cybersecurity: Investigation agents.** Let an agent query logs and draft incident timelines under strict tool policy.

## Frequently asked questions

### How do you let AI agents build data pipelines safely?

Give them a declarative output and no direct path to data: the agent writes Spark Declarative Pipelines specs as a pull request, CI dry-runs them against the real catalog, and execution happens through an identity-pinned Spark Connect ingress with a catalog that authorizes every table operation.

### Do declarative pipelines catch more agent mistakes?

In the safe-spark-agents study (528 runs: 22 tasks, 12 seeds, 2 arms), the Spark Declarative Pipelines dry run caught 79 structural defects before any data was processed, against 0 for the imperative arm. SDP output was 49% fewer lines at about 2.3 times the tokens.

## Sources
- [safe-spark-agents-paper](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/safe-spark-agents-paper)
- [Paper site](https://open-lakehouse.github.io/safe-spark-agents-paper/)

Last updated: 2026-11-21. Canonical page: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/governed-ai-agents

---

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/open-data-sharing

# Open data sharing: Delta Sharing servers over Unity Catalog and open tables

> Share live tables with another organization without copying them or sending files.

Open data sharing is an architecture for giving another organization read access to live lakehouse tables through an open protocol instead of file exports. A Delta Sharing server authenticates the recipient, checks which shares and tables they may read, and returns short-lived URLs or credentials for the underlying files; the recipient reads them with any Delta Sharing client, including pandas, Spark and other engines. Data stays in the provider's storage and the recipient always sees the current version.

## When to use it
- Partners, customers or regulators need recurring access to the same tables.
- You want to stop running file-drop jobs.
- Recipients use different tools than you do.

## When not to
- Write access for recipients: the protocol is read-only.

## Components

| Capability | Component | Role | Version |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source systems | Provider pipelines | Maintain the tables to share |  |
| Batch and SQL | Apache Spark | Provider-side writes |  |
| Catalog and credentials | Unity Catalog OSS | Source of shares and table locations |  |
| Open table format | Delta Lake | Shared tables |  |
| Object storage | Amazon S3 | Provider's bucket; data never moves |  |
| Data sharing | Delta Sharing | Open REST protocol for recipients | server 1.3.10 in open-lakehouse |
| Data sharing | distributary | Composable Rust sharing server with Postgres or SQLite stores |  |

## How data flows
1. **Define a share.** The provider groups tables into a share and grants it to a recipient.
2. **Issue a profile.** The recipient receives a profile file with the server endpoint and a bearer token.
3. **Recipient queries.** The client lists shares and tables and asks to read one, optionally with predicate hints.
4. **Server returns file URLs.** The server checks the grant and returns short-lived URLs for the current table files.
5. **Read directly.** The client reads Parquet files from the provider's storage; nothing is copied into the recipient's platform.

## Run it

### [open-lakehouse/distributary](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/distributary)

OpenSharing and Delta Sharing in Rust: protocol models, client, admin API and a composable sharing server.

```bash
cargo check --workspace --all-features
cargo nextest run --workspace --all-features
```

### [open-lakehouse/unitycatalog-rs](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/unitycatalog-rs)

A catalog that serves a Delta Sharing server alongside the Unity Catalog, Delta and Iceberg REST APIs.

```bash
pip install 'unitycatalog-rs[all]'   # the Python client, the uc CLI, the server and the web UI
uc dev                               # a server on http://localhost:8080, with the web UI
uc catalog list                      # upstream's bin/uc commands
```

### [open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse)

Ships an opt-in Delta Sharing server (1.3.10) on :8443 next to the rest of the stack.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse
cd open-lakehouse

cp .env.example .env       # fill in POSTGRES_*, S3_* placeholders
./lakehouse setup          # validate env, install deps, download ~860MB of JARs
./lakehouse start all      # Spark 4.1 master + worker + Connect server + Kafka
./lakehouse start unity-catalog
./lakehouse start mlflow
./lakehouse status --json  # confirm healthy (incl. spark.connect_grpc_listening)
```

## Caveats
- distributary's README gives developer commands only; its architecture document plans presigned-URL queries, change data feed and recipient tokens.

## Industry use cases
- **Healthcare providers: Research data sharing.** Share de-identified cohorts with a university partner as live tables.
- **Manufacturing: Supplier data exchange.** Share quality and demand tables with suppliers as live tables.
- **Energy and utilities: Regulator and partner sharing.** Share reliability metrics with regulators as live tables.
- **Retail and e-commerce: Supplier collaboration.** Share sell-through and stock tables with suppliers instead of sending reports.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is Delta Sharing?

An open REST protocol, governed with Delta Lake under the Linux Foundation, for sharing live tables across organizations. Recipients read the provider's files through short-lived URLs with any compatible client.

### Do recipients need the same platform as the provider?

No. Clients exist for pandas, Apache Spark and other tools, and the open-lakehouse repos include Rust implementations of the server and client.

## Sources
- [Delta Sharing protocol](https://github.com/delta-io/delta-sharing/blob/main/PROTOCOL.md)
- [distributary](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/distributary)

Last updated: 2026-11-21. Canonical page: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/open-data-sharing

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/laptop-open-lakehouse

# The open lakehouse on a laptop: Spark 4.3, Apache Iceberg, Unity Catalog, Kafka, Airflow, MLflow and an agent, in Docker

> The whole stack, one service at a time, on the machine in front of you.

The open lakehouse on a laptop runs every layer of an open source data platform in Docker on one machine: SeaweedFS as S3-compatible storage, Apache Iceberg tables in Unity Catalog OSS 0.7 through its Iceberg REST endpoint, Apache Spark 4.3 behind a Spark Connect server, Spark Declarative Pipelines for the medallion, Kafka for events, Airflow 3 for scheduling and table maintenance, DuckDB reading the same tables, MLflow for models, and an AI agent on Omnigent with a local model, MCP tools and policies. It exists so a data engineer, a student or an AI agent can build, test and tear down a real lakehouse without a cloud account.

## When to use it
- You want to learn how the layers of an open lakehouse fit together by building them.
- You need a local integration environment with a real catalog and object store.
- You want an AI agent to have a full, disposable stack to work against.

## When not to
- Production: the course's Terraform chapter is illustrative and not applied.
- Teams that need a released Iceberg runtime for Spark 4.3 today: the course builds one from an open Iceberg pull request.

## Components

| Capability | Component | Role | Version |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source systems | Order-event generator | Batch and streaming order events, the course's one dataset |  |
| Batch and file ingestion | Idempotent bronze loader | Appends each batch once |  |
| Event streaming | Apache Kafka | Order events for the streaming chapter | Confluent 7.5.0 images |
| Agent harness and policy | Omnigent | Runs the SDP agent and evaluates ALLOW, DENY and ASK policies on every tool call | 0.22.0 |
| Tools and skills | Model Context Protocol | Named tools: read and write pipeline files, dry-run or run the pipeline, run one SQL statement; no shell |  |
| Models and gateway | Ollama | Local model sdp-qwen3, built from qwen3:14b with a 16K context window |  |
| ML lifecycle | MLflow | Tracks a model trained on gold and logs the gold snapshot id | 3.1.0 |
| Spark Connect sessions | Spark Connect | sc://spark-connect:15002 for every client, the agent included | 4.3.0 |
| Batch and SQL | Apache Spark | Ingestion and queries over Spark Connect | 4.3.0 |
| Declarative pipelines | Spark Declarative Pipelines | Bronze to silver to gold; the agent's output, gated on a dry run | pyspark[pipelines]==4.3.0 |
| Structured Streaming | Apache Spark | Kafka to iceberg.bronze.orders_raw with a checkpoint on S3 | 4.3.0 |
| Other engines | DuckDB | Reads gold through the Iceberg REST endpoint | 1.5.6 |
| Catalog and credentials | Unity Catalog OSS | Writable Iceberg REST catalog; a sandbox namespace for the agent | 0.7.0 |
| Open table format | Apache Iceberg | Bronze, silver and gold tables; snapshots for time travel and rollback | runtime 4.3_2.13 built from apache/iceberg#18749 |
| Object storage | SeaweedFS | s3://lakehouse/warehouse | 4.51 |
| Orchestration | Apache Airflow | Schedules the medallion with backfills | 3.3.2 |
| Table maintenance | Iceberg maintenance procedures | A DAG that runs rewrite_data_files, rewrite_manifests and expire_snapshots |  |

## How data flows
1. **Storage and compute.** SeaweedFS serves the S3 API; Spark 4.3 runs behind a Spark Connect server that every client, including the agent, reaches at sc://.
2. **Tables and catalog.** Unity Catalog OSS 0.7 is the Iceberg REST catalog; tables are named iceberg.<namespace>.<table>, and the agent gets its own sandbox namespace.
3. **Bronze, silver, gold.** Batch loads and a Structured Streaming job land bronze; a Spark Declarative Pipeline derives silver and gold.
4. **Schedule and maintain.** Airflow runs the pipeline with backfills and a second DAG compacts files and expires snapshots.
5. **Serve and learn.** DuckDB reads gold through the same catalog, MLflow trains on it and records the snapshot id.
6. **Hand it to an agent.** An agent on Omnigent with a local model and MCP tools writes pipelines into its sandbox; policies require a passing dry run and ask before code pulls results onto one machine.

## Run it

### [open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass)

The course that builds this stack chapter by chapter, from storage to agents. You write the Compose file yourself; there is no single command.

### [open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse)

The same layers prebuilt, writing Delta Lake into Unity Catalog 0.6.0 with Spark 4.1, started with one script.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse
cd open-lakehouse

cp .env.example .env       # fill in POSTGRES_*, S3_* placeholders
./lakehouse setup          # validate env, install deps, download ~860MB of JARs
./lakehouse start all      # Spark 4.1 master + worker + Connect server + Kafka
./lakehouse start unity-catalog
./lakehouse start mlflow
./lakehouse status --json  # confirm healthy (incl. spark.connect_grpc_listening)
```

## Caveats
- There is no released Iceberg Spark runtime for Spark 4.3; chapter 5.5 builds it from apache/iceberg#18749 as a temporary step.
- Unity Catalog 0.7 or later is required for Iceberg writes through its REST catalog.
- The course recommends 16 GB of RAM; the agent's model needs about 12 GB of memory.
- Older SeaweedFS releases have an S3A _temporary rename bug; the course pins 4.51.
- In open-lakehouse, writes are Delta only: Unity Catalog 0.6.0 serves Iceberg read-only.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I run a full open source lakehouse on a laptop?

Yes. The lakehouse masterclass builds Iceberg tables in Unity Catalog OSS 0.7 on SeaweedFS with Spark 4.3, Kafka, Airflow 3.3.2, DuckDB and MLflow in Docker, and adds an AI agent on Omnigent with a local Ollama model. The open-lakehouse repository offers a prebuilt Delta variant.

### Can an AI agent work on a local lakehouse safely?

Yes. In the masterclass the agent writes only to its own sandbox namespace, uses named MCP tools instead of a shell, and policies require a passing dry run before any pipeline runs.

### How do other engines read the tables?

Through Unity Catalog's Iceberg REST endpoint. DuckDB attaches it and reads the gold tables Spark wrote, without copies.

## Sources
- [lakehouse-masterclass](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass)
- [open-lakehouse docs/compatibility.md](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse/blob/main/docs/compatibility.md)

# Policy pushdown and open lineage: Cedar policies compiled to CEL, enforced in Spark and DataFusion, with OpenLineage

> Write access rules once, enforce them inside every engine, and record where every column came from.

Policy pushdown and open lineage is a governance architecture for multi-engine lakehouses. Access rules are authored once in the Cedar policy language, compiled to portable CEL expressions, and enforced inside each query engine's plan as row filters and column masks, so no engine depends on SQL views or per-engine rewrites. Alongside, every job emits OpenLineage events, which are stored as lakehouse tables and served through a lineage API, so auditors can trace a published number back to its sources.

## When to use it
- Several engines read the same sensitive tables.
- You need row filters and column masks that cannot be bypassed by choosing a different engine.
- Regulators or auditors ask where a value came from.

## When not to
- Production lineage storage today without evaluation: headwaters describes itself as experimental and recommends Marquez for production.

## Components

| Capability | Component | Role | Version |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source systems | Policy authors | Write Cedar policies and tag templates |  |
| Batch and SQL | Apache Spark | Enforcement as Catalyst rules | 4.2 plugin |
| Other engines | Apache DataFusion | Enforcement as plan rewrites | 53.1 |
| Catalog and credentials | Unity Catalog OSS | Policy decision point resolving tags | 0.4.1 in the demo |
| Open table format | Apache Iceberg | Lineage event tables, written through Lakekeeper (Delta also supported) |  |
| Object storage | RustFS | Demo object store |  |
| Access control and policy | Cedar | Policy language; deny always wins | cedar-policy 4 |
| Access control and policy | policast | Compiles Cedar to CEL and injects enforcement into the physical plan |  |
| Access control and policy | breakwater | Row filters and column masks inside the DataFusion planner |  |
| Lineage | OpenLineage | Lineage events from every job, column level from Spark |  |
| Lineage | open-lineage-connect | Ingests events and writes them to Delta and Iceberg tables |  |
| Lineage | headwaters | Lineage read API and UI |  |

## How data flows
1. **Author once.** A policy author writes Cedar policies, including tag-based templates that apply to every column tagged, for example, as PHI.
2. **Compile.** policast compiles the policies to CEL expressions that any engine can evaluate.
3. **Enforce in the plan.** Spark applies them as Catalyst rules and DataFusion as plan rewrites, so filters and masks run inside the query, not in a view.
4. **Emit lineage.** A Spark 4 plugin emits OpenLineage events with column-level lineage for each job.
5. **Store lineage as tables.** An ingest service writes the events to Delta or Iceberg tables, which a lineage API and UI read.

## Run it

### [open-lakehouse/policast](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/policast)

Author governance once in Cedar, compile it to portable CEL, and push enforcement into Spark and DataFusion physical plans.

```bash
cp docker/.env.example .env
docker compose up -d sidecar
docker compose --profile demo run --rm datafusion-demo

# Same policies enforced on Spark (Catalyst rules, no sidecar):
docker compose --profile spark run --rm spark-demo   # or: just spark-demo
```

### [open-lakehouse/open-lineage-connect](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lineage-connect)

OpenLineage end to end: a Go ingest service, a Rust service that writes events to Delta and Iceberg tables, and a Spark 4 plugin for column-level lineage.

```bash
make docker-compose-up        # builds both images, starts both services + MinIO
curl -sf http://localhost:8090/health
curl -sf http://localhost:8091/health
make docker-compose-down      # tears it down and removes the Delta volume
```

### [open-lakehouse/breakwater](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/breakwater)

Cedar fine-grained access control for DataFusion, with OCI-distributed policy bundles and a policy decision point service.

### [open-lakehouse/headwaters](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/headwaters)

Experimental Rust OpenLineage service with a Marquez-inspired read API and UI.

## Caveats
- In policast, deny always wins and grants never bypass column masks.
- headwaters is experimental and not a drop-in Marquez replacement.
- The policast demo pins Unity Catalog 0.4.1 as its policy decision point.

## Industry use cases
- **Banking: Regulatory reporting from one copy.** Build liquidity and capital reports from conformed silver tables with lineage an auditor can follow.
- **Healthcare providers: Patient-level access policy.** Enforce row filters and column masks on PHI the same way in every engine that reads the tables.
- **Telecommunications: Subscriber data protection.** Mask subscriber identifiers for analysts and keep lineage for regulators.
- **Cybersecurity: Least-privilege access to logs.** Restrict sensitive log fields by role in every engine.

## Frequently asked questions

### How do you enforce the same access policy in Spark and other engines?

Compile one policy source into an engine-neutral form and inject it into each engine's query plan. policast compiles Cedar policies to CEL and enforces them as Catalyst rules in Spark and as plan rewrites in DataFusion.

### What is OpenLineage?

An open standard, hosted by the LF AI & Data Foundation, for lineage events that describe jobs, runs and the datasets they read and write. Spark, Airflow, Flink and dbt have integrations.

### Can lineage be stored in the lakehouse itself?

Yes. open-lineage-connect writes OpenLineage events to Delta tables, Iceberg tables through a REST catalog, or both.

## Sources
- [policast README](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/policast#readme)
- [open-lineage-connect README](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lineage-connect#readme)
- [OpenLineage](https://openlineage.io)

Last updated: 2026-11-21. Canonical page: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/policy-and-lineage

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/semantic-layer

# Semantic layer with Spark metric views: Metrics declared in YAML, served over Spark Connect to BI, notebooks and agents

> Define revenue once. Every dashboard, notebook and agent gets the same number.

A semantic layer is the set of governed metric and dimension definitions that sit between tables and the tools that query them. In open source Apache Spark, a metric view declares measures and dimensions in YAML over a source table; consumers query it with the MEASURE() function and Spark expands the definition at query time. Served over Spark Connect or JDBC, the same definitions answer dashboards, notebooks and AI agents, so a metric cannot drift between tools.

## When to use it
- Different teams report different numbers for the same metric.
- You want AI agents to answer questions from governed definitions instead of writing raw SQL.

## When not to
- Spark versions before metric views shipped; the reference demo is verified on Spark 4.2.0.

## Components

| Capability | Component | Role | Version |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source systems | Gold tables | Facts and dimensions to measure |  |
| Spark Connect sessions | Spark Connect | Remote access for clients and agents |  |
| Batch and SQL | Apache Spark | Expands MEASURE() at query time | 4.2.0 |
| Catalog and credentials | Hive Metastore | Registers the metric view in the demo |  |
| Open table format | Delta Lake | Source tables |  |
| Semantic layer | Spark metric views | YAML measures and dimensions |  |
| Dashboards and notebooks | Apache Superset | Dashboards over the metric view |  |

## How data flows
1. **Declare metrics.** Write measures and dimensions in YAML over a source table.
2. **Register.** Create the metric view in the catalog.
3. **Query with MEASURE().** Clients select dimensions and MEASURE(metric); Spark expands the definition and aggregates at the requested grain.
4. **Serve everyone.** Dashboards connect over JDBC or Spark Connect, and agents use the same views as tools.

## Run it

### [lisancao/spark-demos](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos)

Demo 01_metrics_views: eight metric view examples, a doctor script and a grammar probe, verified on Spark 4.2.0.

## Caveats
- The reference demo is verified on Spark 4.2.0 and awaits official Spark 4.3 images for re-verification.

## Industry use cases
- **Banking: Analyst questions in plain language.** Let relationship managers ask about balances and products through governed metric definitions.
- **Manufacturing: OEE dashboards with one definition.** Define availability, performance and quality once and query them from BI and agents.
- **Retail and e-commerce: One definition of margin.** Define revenue, margin and sell-through once for BI, notebooks and agents.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does open source Spark have a semantic layer?

Yes. Spark metric views declare measures and dimensions in YAML over a table, and queries use the MEASURE() function to evaluate them.

### Why give AI agents a semantic layer?

Because an agent querying metric views uses the governed definition of each metric instead of inventing its own SQL, so its answers match the dashboards.

## Sources
- [spark-demos 01_metrics_views](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos/tree/main/demos/01_metrics_views)

Last updated: 2026-11-21. Canonical page: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/semantic-layer

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/ml-lifecycle

# ML and GenAI lifecycle on the lakehouse: MLflow tracking, registry and AI Gateway over open tables

> Every model run points at the exact table version it was trained on.

The ML lifecycle on an open lakehouse ties experiments, models and GenAI traces to versioned tables. Features are built by Spark from silver and gold tables in an open format; each MLflow run records parameters, metrics, artifacts and the table snapshot or version it trained on; the MLflow model registry promotes versions; and the MLflow AI Gateway fronts model providers for GenAI applications. Because tables support time travel, any run can be reproduced against the exact data it saw.

## When to use it
- You need to reproduce a model from months ago.
- You train on lakehouse tables and want lineage from data to model.
- You run GenAI applications and want tracing and evaluation in the same place.

## When not to
- Low-latency online feature serving by itself: pair it with the real-time streaming pattern and a key-value store.

## Components

| Capability | Component | Role | Version |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source systems | Gold feature tables | Training data |  |
| ML lifecycle | MLflow | Tracking, registry, tracing, evaluation and AI Gateway | 3.14.0 in open-lakehouse; 3.1.0 in the course |
| Batch and SQL | Apache Spark | Feature engineering and batch scoring |  |
| Catalog and credentials | Unity Catalog OSS | Tables, and in the course, the catalog the run reads through |  |
| Open table format | Apache Iceberg | Snapshot ids give reproducible training sets |  |
| Orchestration | Apache Airflow | Retraining schedules |  |
| Dashboards and notebooks | Jupyter | Experiments |  |

## How data flows
1. **Build features.** Spark reads gold tables and writes a feature table.
2. **Record the data version.** The training run logs the table's snapshot id or version to MLflow alongside parameters and metrics.
3. **Register.** A good run's model is registered and promoted in the MLflow model registry.
4. **Serve and trace.** Applications call models and providers through the MLflow AI Gateway; traces land back in MLflow for evaluation.

## Run it

### [open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse)

Runs MLflow 3.14.0 tracking (:5000) and AI Gateway (:5001) next to Spark, Delta and Unity Catalog.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse
cd open-lakehouse

cp .env.example .env       # fill in POSTGRES_*, S3_* placeholders
./lakehouse setup          # validate env, install deps, download ~860MB of JARs
./lakehouse start all      # Spark 4.1 master + worker + Connect server + Kafka
./lakehouse start unity-catalog
./lakehouse start mlflow
./lakehouse status --json  # confirm healthy (incl. spark.connect_grpc_listening)
```

### [open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass)

Chapter 12 trains a model on gold and logs the gold Iceberg snapshot id to MLflow.

## Caveats
- MLflow 3.x matches --allowed-hosts exactly; the open-lakehouse stack sets localhost:5000 explicitly.

## Industry use cases
- **Banking: Credit risk model lifecycle.** Track, register and compare probability-of-default models trained on governed features.
- **Healthcare providers: Readmission risk models.** Track experiments and promote models with a registry that records the training data version.
- **Energy and utilities: Load forecasting.** Train and track forecast models on years of interval data plus weather.
- **Retail and e-commerce: Demand forecasting.** Train store-by-SKU forecasts and track which model version produced each order.
- **Telecommunications: Churn models.** Train and track churn models on usage, care and billing features.

## Frequently asked questions

### How do I make an ML model reproducible on a lakehouse?

Log the table snapshot id (Iceberg) or version (Delta Lake) used for training to the MLflow run; time travel then lets you read exactly that data again.

### Is MLflow open source?

Yes. MLflow is Apache-2.0 licensed and hosted by the Linux Foundation.

## Sources
- [MLflow docs](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/)

Last updated: 2026-11-21. Canonical page: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/ml-lifecycle

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/arrow-native-serving

# Arrow-native serving: Arrow Flight SQL and Spark Connect clients over lakehouse tables

> Results leave as Arrow columns, not rows, in whatever language the client speaks.

Arrow-native serving delivers lakehouse query results as Apache Arrow record batches over gRPC instead of row-by-row JDBC. Two open protocols do this: Arrow Flight SQL, a generic SQL-over-Flight protocol, and Spark Connect, Spark's client-server protocol. A Flight SQL server built on Apache DataFusion can answer queries over Delta tables with policy enforcement and lineage built in, while Spark Connect lets thin clients in Python, Go, Rust, Swift and other languages send plans to a remote Spark and hand the Arrow results straight to DuckDB or Polars.

## When to use it
- Clients pull large result sets into Python, Rust or other analytical tools.
- You want to query the lakehouse from a language without a JVM.
- You want policy and lineage enforced at the serving edge.

## When not to
- Clients that only speak ODBC or JDBC: put a Flight SQL JDBC driver or a SQL gateway in front.

## Components

| Capability | Component | Role | Version |
|---|---|---|---|
| Spark Connect sessions | Spark Connect | gRPC protocol for Spark clients |  |
| Spark Connect sessions | Spark Connect clients | Python, Scala, Go, Rust, OCaml, Swift clients |  |
| Batch and SQL | Apache Spark | Remote engine behind Spark Connect | 4.2.0 in the demos |
| Other engines | Apache DataFusion | Query engine inside the Flight SQL server | 55 |
| Other engines | DuckDB | Joins Arrow results locally |  |
| Catalog and credentials | Unity Catalog OSS | Resolves tables and vends credentials |  |
| Open table format | Delta Lake | Tables served |  |
| Access control and policy | breakwater | Cedar enforcement in the DataFusion planner |  |
| Lineage | OpenLineage | Lineage emitted per query |  |
| Apps and APIs | hydrofoil | Flight SQL server with Cedar policy and OpenLineage |  |
| Apps and APIs | Arrow Flight SQL | Protocol |  |

## How data flows
1. **Client sends a query or plan.** A Flight SQL client sends SQL, or a Spark Connect client sends an unresolved logical plan over gRPC.
2. **Server resolves tables.** The server resolves table names through the catalog and obtains storage access.
3. **Policy applies.** In hydrofoil, Cedar policies are enforced inside the DataFusion plan before execution.
4. **Arrow streams back.** Results stream to the client as Arrow record batches.
5. **Zero-copy downstream.** The client hands the same Arrow batches to DuckDB or Polars without conversion.

## Run it

### [open-lakehouse/hydrofoil](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/hydrofoil)

A Flight SQL server over open-table-format tables, built on DataFusion 55 with Cedar policy enforcement, OpenLineage and OpenTelemetry tracing.

### [lisancao/spark-demos](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos)

Demos 02 (Spark Connect setup), 08 (OCaml client) and 09 (Rust client with DuckDB 2.0 and Polars on the same Arrow batches).

## Caveats
- hydrofoil's README does not yet document running the Flight SQL server; its architecture is recorded in docs/adr.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the difference between Arrow Flight SQL and Spark Connect?

Both stream Apache Arrow over gRPC. Flight SQL is a generic SQL protocol any engine can implement; Spark Connect carries Spark's own logical plans, so clients get the full DataFrame API of a remote Spark.

### Can I use Spark from Rust or Go?

Yes, through Spark Connect clients. spark-demos demo 09 uses the Rust client and passes the Arrow results to DuckDB and Polars.

## Sources
- [Arrow Flight SQL](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/FlightSql.html)
- [Spark Connect overview](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/spark-connect-overview.html)

Last updated: 2026-11-21. Canonical page: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/arrow-native-serving

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/cloud-deployment-aws

# Self-hosted catalog on AWS: Unity Catalog OSS on ECS Fargate with Neon Postgres and S3, in Terraform

> The open catalog in your own AWS account, with no static storage keys.

A self-hosted open catalog on AWS runs Unity Catalog OSS as a container on Amazon ECS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer, keeps catalog metadata in a managed Postgres database, stores configuration on EFS and secrets in AWS Secrets Manager, and vends credentials for an S3 data bucket through a bucket-scoped IAM role instead of static keys. Everything is declared in Terraform, so the catalog can be recreated in another account or region from code.

## When to use it
- You want an open catalog in your own cloud account.
- Data residency or sovereignty rules out a hosted service.

## When not to
- A full compute stack: this reference deploys the catalog server; compute is deployed separately.

## Components

| Capability | Component | Role | Version |
|---|---|---|---|
| Batch and SQL | Apache Spark | Any engine with a Unity Catalog or Iceberg REST client |  |
| Catalog and credentials | Unity Catalog OSS | Catalog server, digest-pinned and mirrored to ECR | 0.7.0 |
| Catalog and credentials | Neon | Postgres for catalog metadata |  |
| Object storage | Amazon S3 | Data bucket reached through a bucket-scoped storage role |  |
| Runtime, CI/CD and IaC | Amazon ECS on Fargate | Runs the server in a two-AZ VPC behind a public ALB |  |
| Runtime, CI/CD and IaC | Terraform | Declares the whole deployment | >= 1.11, AWS provider ~> 6.45 |

## How data flows
1. **Prepare a profile.** just init-profile and just doctor check AWS credentials and tooling.
2. **Sync state and secrets.** Terraform state and the Neon connection secret are synced into the account.
3. **Deploy.** just deploy uc-server applies Terraform: VPC, ALB, ECS service, EFS and the storage role.
4. **Bootstrap.** The bootstrap step creates the storage credential, the unity catalog and the unity.default schema.

## Run it

### [open-lakehouse/terraform-deploy-oss](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/terraform-deploy-oss)

Terraform and scripts for deploying open source lakehouse services to the cloud, starting with Unity Catalog on AWS.

```bash
just init-profile prod
just doctor
just sync terraform-state
just sync neon-secret
just deploy uc-server
```

### [open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse)

terraform/ holds AWS deployment for the rest of the stack, including Spark and MLflow on ECS (just deploy spark-ecs, just deploy mlflow-ecs).

```bash
git clone https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse
cd open-lakehouse

cp .env.example .env       # fill in POSTGRES_*, S3_* placeholders
./lakehouse setup          # validate env, install deps, download ~860MB of JARs
./lakehouse start all      # Spark 4.1 master + worker + Connect server + Kafka
./lakehouse start unity-catalog
./lakehouse start mlflow
./lakehouse status --json  # confirm healthy (incl. spark.connect_grpc_listening)
```

## Caveats
- Upgrading Unity Catalog from 0.6.0 or earlier needs a schema change: ALTER TABLE uc_properties ALTER COLUMN property_value TYPE text;
- Unity Catalog 0.7.0 permanently deletes dropped managed table files after seven days.
- The default ingress CIDR is 0.0.0.0/0; narrow it before production.
- During the measured v0.7.0 cutover in the sandbox, 5 of 491 requests returned 502 within 8 seconds (docs/unitycatalog/observability.md).

## Industry use cases
- **Energy and utilities: Self-hosted on AWS.** Run the open stack in the utility's own cloud account with infrastructure as code.

## Frequently asked questions

### How do I deploy Unity Catalog OSS on AWS?

terraform-deploy-oss runs Unity Catalog 0.7.0 on ECS Fargate behind an ALB, with Neon Postgres for metadata, EFS for configuration and a bucket-scoped IAM role for S3, deployed with just deploy uc-server.

## Sources
- [terraform-deploy-oss](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/terraform-deploy-oss)

Last updated: 2026-11-21. Canonical page: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/cloud-deployment-aws

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/serverless-lakehouse-services

# Serverless lakehouse services: Catalog and lineage as Neon Functions on branchable Postgres

> Every pull request gets its own catalog, database and bucket.

Serverless lakehouse services package the control plane of an open lakehouse (the catalog, the lineage service and the sharing server) as functions that run per database branch. In luminescent-lakehouse, Rust services built on axum are compiled to Node-API addons and deployed as Neon Functions; each Neon branch gets its own Postgres schema and storage bucket, so a pull request preview has a full, isolated catalog and lineage service that disappears with the branch.

## When to use it
- You want preview environments with their own catalog per pull request.
- You want to run lakehouse control-plane services without operating servers.

## When not to
- Data-plane compute: engines still run elsewhere and talk to these services over HTTP.

## Components

| Capability | Component | Role | Version |
|---|---|---|---|
| Catalog and credentials | Neon | Per-branch Postgres and storage bucket |  |
| Catalog and credentials | unitycatalog-rs | Catalog function (mangrove server) |  |
| Open table format | Delta Lake | Managed tables under s3://lakehouse/managed |  |
| Lineage | headwaters | OpenLineage ingest with Marquez-compatible reads |  |
| Data sharing | distributary | Sharing function; built and tested, not yet deployed |  |

## How data flows
1. **Build.** Each Rust service is compiled to a linux-arm64 Node-API addon and bundled within Neon's size limits.
2. **Migrate a branch.** Deploying to a Neon branch runs the database migrations for that branch.
3. **Deploy functions.** The catalog and lineage functions are applied to the branch from neon.ts.
4. **Promote.** Pull requests get preview branches, merges deploy to staging, and production needs manual approval.

## Run it

### [open-lakehouse/luminescent-lakehouse](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/luminescent-lakehouse)

Deploys open-lakehouse services (Unity Catalog, OpenLineage, OpenSharing) to Neon as functions.

```bash
just test <fn>         # host-native addon behind the fetch handler, node --test
just build <fn>        # linux-arm64 bundle + zip, gated on Neon's size limits
just test-arm64 <fn>   # the deployable bundle in node:24-bookworm-slim
just deploy <branch>   # migrate a Neon branch and apply neon.ts to it
```

## Caveats
- The opensharing function builds and passes tests but is not in neon.ts yet; only the catalog and lineage functions deploy.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can a data catalog run serverless?

Yes. luminescent-lakehouse runs a Unity Catalog implementation and an OpenLineage service as Neon Functions, with a separate Postgres branch and bucket per environment.

## Sources
- [luminescent-lakehouse](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/luminescent-lakehouse)

Last updated: 2026-11-21. Canonical page: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/serverless-lakehouse-services

# Open source data architecture for Banking

Banks move core banking ledgers, card authorizations and payment messages into open tables so fraud, risk and regulatory reporting read one governed copy instead of a mart per team.

## Source systems

| System | How data arrives |
|---|---|
| Core banking system | Nightly batch extracts plus CDC from the ledger database |
| Card authorization switch | Streaming, one event per authorization |
| Payment hub | Streaming ISO 20022 messages |
| CRM and digital channels | Hourly batch and clickstream events |
| Market and reference data feeds | Intraday batch files |

## Data formats and standards

| Format | Standards body | What it carries |
|---|---|---|
| [ISO 20022](https://www.iso20022.org) | ISO | XML message standard for payments and securities |
| [SWIFT MT](https://www.swift.com/standards/category-7-mt) | Swift | Legacy FIN messages still exchanged during the MX migration |
| [ISO 8583](https://www.iso.org/standard/79451.html) | ISO | Card transaction message format |

## Medallion layers in this industry's terms
- **Bronze:** Raw ledger extracts and payment messages
- **Silver:** Conformed accounts, customers and transactions
- **Gold:** Exposure, liquidity and fraud features

## Use cases and the architecture for each
- **Real-time card fraud scoring.** Score each authorization against recent account behaviour before the switch times out. Architecture: [Real-time streaming with Spark Real-Time Mode](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/real-time-streaming).
- **Regulatory reporting from one copy.** Build liquidity and capital reports from conformed silver tables with lineage an auditor can follow. Architecture: [Policy pushdown and open lineage](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/policy-and-lineage).
- **Core banking CDC into the lakehouse.** Keep a current and historical (SCD type 2) view of accounts without full nightly reloads. Architecture: [Change data capture with SCD type 2](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/change-data-capture).
- **Credit risk model lifecycle.** Track, register and compare probability-of-default models trained on governed features. Architecture: [ML and GenAI lifecycle on the lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/ml-lifecycle).
- **Analyst questions in plain language.** Let relationship managers ask about balances and products through governed metric definitions. Architecture: [Semantic layer with Spark metric views](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/semantic-layer).

Canonical page: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/industries/banking

---

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/industries/payments-fintech

# Open source data architecture for Payments and fintech

Payment processors and fintechs run on event streams; the lakehouse holds the durable history that fraud models, reconciliation and merchant analytics read.

## Source systems

| System | How data arrives |
|---|---|
| Payment gateway and acquirer | Streaming authorization and capture events |
| ACH and real-time payment rails | Batch files and streaming ISO 20022 |
| Application databases | CDC through Debezium |
| Mobile app events | Streaming clickstream |

## Data formats and standards

| Format | Standards body | What it carries |
|---|---|---|
| [ISO 8583](https://www.iso.org/standard/79451.html) | ISO | Card network messages |
| [ISO 20022](https://www.iso20022.org) | ISO | Real-time and cross-border payment messages |
| [Nacha ACH file format](https://www.nacha.org) | Nacha | Fixed-width US ACH batch files |

## Medallion layers in this industry's terms
- **Bronze:** Raw gateway events and rail files
- **Silver:** One row per payment with its lifecycle state
- **Gold:** Merchant settlement, chargeback and fraud features

## Use cases and the architecture for each
- **Sub-second fraud features.** Maintain velocity counters per card and device and serve them while the payment is still in flight. Architecture: [Real-time streaming with Spark Real-Time Mode](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/real-time-streaming).
- **Ledger reconciliation.** Match gateway, processor and bank files every day and surface the breaks. Architecture: [Batch medallion with Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/batch-medallion).
- **Streaming payment history into tables.** Land every gateway event in a bronze table and keep silver current within seconds. Architecture: [Streaming medallion](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/streaming-medallion).
- **Migrating a Flink fraud job to Spark.** Port keyed state and windows to Spark and measure whether latency holds. Architecture: [Real-time streaming with Spark Real-Time Mode](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/real-time-streaming).
- **Governed agent for merchant support.** Let an agent answer settlement questions with tools limited by policy. Architecture: [Governed AI agents for data engineering](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/governed-ai-agents).

Canonical page: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/industries/payments-fintech

---

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/industries/healthcare

# Open source data architecture for Healthcare providers

Health systems pull EHR, claims and device data into open tables mapped to a common data model, with strict access policy on every column that identifies a patient.

## Source systems

| System | How data arrives |
|---|---|
| Electronic health record | HL7 v2 feeds, FHIR APIs and bulk exports |
| Claims and billing | Batch X12 837 and 835 files |
| Imaging archive (PACS) | DICOM objects and metadata |
| Bedside and remote monitoring devices | Streaming vitals |

## Data formats and standards

| Format | Standards body | What it carries |
|---|---|---|
| [HL7 FHIR](https://hl7.org/fhir/) | HL7 International | REST resources and bulk NDJSON exports for clinical data |
| [HL7 v2](https://www.hl7.org/implement/standards/product_brief.cfm?product_id=185) | HL7 International | Pipe-delimited ADT, ORU and ORM messages |
| [DICOM](https://www.dicomstandard.org) | NEMA (DICOM Standards Committee) | Medical imaging objects and metadata |
| [OMOP CDM](https://ohdsi.github.io/CommonDataModel/) | OHDSI | Common data model for observational research |
| [X12 837/835](https://x12.org) | X12 | Claim and remittance transactions |

## Medallion layers in this industry's terms
- **Bronze:** Raw HL7, FHIR bundles and claim files
- **Silver:** OMOP-conformed persons, visits, conditions and measurements
- **Gold:** Quality measures, readmission risk and capacity dashboards

## Use cases and the architecture for each
- **Patient-level access policy.** Enforce row filters and column masks on PHI the same way in every engine that reads the tables. Architecture: [Policy pushdown and open lineage](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/policy-and-lineage).
- **Real-time deterioration alerts.** Score streaming vitals against early-warning rules and push alerts to care teams. Architecture: [Real-time streaming with Spark Real-Time Mode](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/real-time-streaming).
- **FHIR bulk export to OMOP.** Land FHIR NDJSON in bronze and transform it into the OMOP common data model. Architecture: [Batch medallion with Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/batch-medallion).
- **Readmission risk models.** Track experiments and promote models with a registry that records the training data version. Architecture: [ML and GenAI lifecycle on the lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/ml-lifecycle).
- **Research data sharing.** Share de-identified cohorts with a university partner as live tables. Architecture: [Open data sharing](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/open-data-sharing).

Canonical page: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/industries/healthcare

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/industries/manufacturing

# Open source data architecture for Manufacturing

Plants stream machine telemetry from the shop floor, join it with MES and ERP records, and use the result for predictive maintenance, quality and OEE.

## Source systems

| System | How data arrives |
|---|---|
| PLCs and SCADA via OPC UA | Streaming sensor tags |
| Plant historian | Batch backfill and streaming |
| Manufacturing execution system (MES) | CDC |
| ERP | Nightly batch |

## Data formats and standards

| Format | Standards body | What it carries |
|---|---|---|
| [OPC UA](https://opcfoundation.org/about/opc-technologies/opc-ua/) | OPC Foundation | Industrial machine-to-machine protocol and information model |
| [MQTT](https://mqtt.org) | OASIS | Lightweight publish/subscribe messaging for devices |
| [Sparkplug](https://sparkplug.eclipse.org) | Eclipse Foundation | MQTT topic and payload specification for industrial data |
| [ISA-95](https://www.isa.org/standards-and-publications/isa-standards/isa-95-standard) | ISA | Model for enterprise and control system integration |

## Medallion layers in this industry's terms
- **Bronze:** Raw tag readings and MES events
- **Silver:** Asset-aligned time series on the ISA-95 hierarchy
- **Gold:** OEE, scrap rate and failure predictions

## Use cases and the architecture for each
- **Predictive maintenance.** Compute rolling sensor features per asset and score failure risk continuously. Architecture: [Real-time streaming with Spark Real-Time Mode](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/real-time-streaming).
- **Telemetry into tables.** Land MQTT and OPC UA readings in bronze and keep asset-level silver current. Architecture: [Streaming medallion](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/streaming-medallion).
- **OEE dashboards with one definition.** Define availability, performance and quality once and query them from BI and agents. Architecture: [Semantic layer with Spark metric views](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/semantic-layer).
- **Supplier data exchange.** Share quality and demand tables with suppliers as live tables. Architecture: [Open data sharing](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/open-data-sharing).
- **Quality and scrap analytics.** Join MES quality checks with ERP orders every shift to find where scrap comes from. Architecture: [Batch medallion with Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/batch-medallion).

Canonical page: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/industries/manufacturing

# Open source data architecture for Energy and utilities

Utilities combine smart meter interval data, grid telemetry and asset records for load forecasting, outage response and regulatory filings.

## Source systems

| System | How data arrives |
|---|---|
| Advanced metering infrastructure (AMI) | Interval reads every 15 minutes, batch and streaming |
| SCADA and substation automation | Streaming telemetry |
| Outage management system | Streaming events |
| GIS and asset registry | Batch |

## Data formats and standards

| Format | Standards body | What it carries |
|---|---|---|
| [IEC 61850](https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/6028) | IEC | Substation automation communication |
| [CIM (IEC 61970 / 61968)](https://cimug.ucaiug.org) | IEC | Common information model for grid and distribution |
| [Green Button](https://www.greenbuttonalliance.org) | Green Button Alliance | Customer energy usage data exchange |
| [DNP3 (IEEE 1815)](https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/1815/10003/) | IEEE | SCADA protocol for utilities |

## Medallion layers in this industry's terms
- **Bronze:** Raw interval reads and SCADA points
- **Silver:** Validated, estimated and edited (VEE) meter data on the CIM network model
- **Gold:** Load forecasts, outage KPIs and rate-case reports

## Use cases and the architecture for each
- **Load forecasting.** Train and track forecast models on years of interval data plus weather. Architecture: [ML and GenAI lifecycle on the lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/ml-lifecycle).
- **Meter data at scale.** Process billions of interval reads a day through bronze, VEE silver and billing gold. Architecture: [Batch medallion with Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/batch-medallion).
- **Outage detection from streaming telemetry.** Correlate last-gasp meter events and SCADA alarms within seconds. Architecture: [Real-time streaming with Spark Real-Time Mode](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/real-time-streaming).
- **Regulator and partner sharing.** Share reliability metrics with regulators as live tables. Architecture: [Open data sharing](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/open-data-sharing).
- **Self-hosted on AWS.** Run the open stack in the utility's own cloud account with infrastructure as code. Architecture: [Self-hosted catalog on AWS](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/cloud-deployment-aws).

Canonical page: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/industries/energy-utilities

# Open source data architecture for Retail and e-commerce

Retailers and online stores bring point-of-sale, clickstream, inventory, supply chain and loyalty data together for demand forecasting, replenishment, personalization and fraud.

## Source systems

| System | How data arrives |
|---|---|
| Point-of-sale systems | Streaming baskets, end-of-day batch |
| Web and app clickstream | Streaming events |
| Inventory and warehouse management | CDC |
| Supplier EDI | Batch X12 or EDIFACT documents |
| Loyalty and CRM | Batch |

## Data formats and standards

| Format | Standards body | What it carries |
|---|---|---|
| [GS1 EPCIS](https://www.gs1.org/standards/epcis) | GS1 | Supply chain visibility events |
| [GTIN](https://www.gs1.org/standards/id-keys/gtin) | GS1 | Global trade item numbers that key the product master |
| [ANSI X12 (850, 856, 810)](https://x12.org) | X12 | Purchase orders, ship notices and invoices |
| [UN/EDIFACT](https://unece.org/trade/uncefact/introducing-unedifact) | UNECE | International EDI messages |
| [CloudEvents](https://cloudevents.io) | CNCF | Common envelope for clickstream and order events |

## Medallion layers in this industry's terms
- **Bronze:** Raw baskets, EDI documents and stock snapshots
- **Silver:** Sales, inventory and orders keyed by GTIN and store
- **Gold:** Forecasts, replenishment orders and customer segments

## Use cases and the architecture for each
- **Demand forecasting.** Train store-by-SKU forecasts and track which model version produced each order. Architecture: [ML and GenAI lifecycle on the lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/ml-lifecycle).
- **Real-time inventory.** Keep stock positions current from POS and warehouse events so online orders do not oversell. Architecture: [Streaming medallion](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/streaming-medallion).
- **Supplier collaboration.** Share sell-through and stock tables with suppliers instead of sending reports. Architecture: [Open data sharing](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/open-data-sharing).
- **One definition of margin.** Define revenue, margin and sell-through once for BI, notebooks and agents. Architecture: [Semantic layer with Spark metric views](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/semantic-layer).
- **In-session recommendations.** Update product recommendations while the shopper is still browsing. Architecture: [Real-time streaming with Spark Real-Time Mode](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/real-time-streaming).
- **Clickstream to sessions.** Sessionize web and app events with watermarks and land them as tables for funnel analysis. Architecture: [Streaming medallion](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/streaming-medallion).

Canonical page: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/industries/retail-ecommerce

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/industries/telecommunications

# Open source data architecture for Telecommunications

Operators collect network performance counters, call detail records and customer data for network planning, churn and service assurance.

## Source systems

| System | How data arrives |
|---|---|
| Network elements and OSS | Streaming performance counters and alarms |
| Mediation (CDRs and xDRs) | Batch files every few minutes |
| BSS: billing and CRM | CDC |

## Data formats and standards

| Format | Standards body | What it carries |
|---|---|---|
| [3GPP charging data records](https://www.3gpp.org/specifications-technologies) | 3GPP | CDR formats defined in TS 32.297 and related specs |
| [TM Forum Open APIs](https://www.tmforum.org/oda/open-apis/) | TM Forum | Standard APIs for BSS and OSS integration |

## Medallion layers in this industry's terms
- **Bronze:** Raw counters, alarms and CDR files
- **Silver:** Cell, subscriber and session-level facts
- **Gold:** Network KPIs, churn scores and capacity plans

## Use cases and the architecture for each
- **Service assurance.** Correlate alarms and KPI drops across cells within seconds. Architecture: [Real-time streaming with Spark Real-Time Mode](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/real-time-streaming).
- **CDR processing.** Process mediation files into rated usage tables every few minutes. Architecture: [Streaming medallion](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/streaming-medallion).
- **Churn models.** Train and track churn models on usage, care and billing features. Architecture: [ML and GenAI lifecycle on the lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/ml-lifecycle).
- **Subscriber data protection.** Mask subscriber identifiers for analysts and keep lineage for regulators. Architecture: [Policy pushdown and open lineage](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/policy-and-lineage).
- **Network planning on many engines.** Run heavy jobs in Spark and interactive exploration in Trino against one catalog. Architecture: [One catalog, many engines](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/multi-engine-catalog).

Canonical page: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/industries/telecommunications

---

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/industries/cybersecurity

# Open source data architecture for Cybersecurity

Security teams keep years of logs in open tables at object-storage prices and run detections, hunts and investigations over them with several engines.

## Source systems

| System | How data arrives |
|---|---|
| Endpoint, identity and network logs | Streaming |
| Cloud audit logs | Streaming and batch |
| Threat intelligence feeds | Batch STIX bundles |

## Data formats and standards

| Format | Standards body | What it carries |
|---|---|---|
| [OCSF](https://ocsf.io) | OCSF project | Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework for normalized security events |
| [STIX / TAXII](https://oasis-open.github.io/cti-documentation/) | OASIS | Threat intelligence objects and transport |
| [Sigma](https://sigmahq.io) | SigmaHQ | Generic detection rule format |

## Medallion layers in this industry's terms
- **Bronze:** Raw logs per source
- **Silver:** OCSF-normalized events
- **Gold:** Detections, incidents and entity timelines

## Use cases and the architecture for each
- **Streaming detections.** Evaluate detection rules on normalized events within seconds of arrival. Architecture: [Real-time streaming with Spark Real-Time Mode](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/real-time-streaming).
- **Security data lake.** Normalize every source to OCSF in silver and keep years of history cheaply. Architecture: [Streaming medallion](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/streaming-medallion).
- **Threat hunting with any engine.** Hunt in DuckDB or Trino over the same tables that Spark writes. Architecture: [One catalog, many engines](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/multi-engine-catalog).
- **Least-privilege access to logs.** Restrict sensitive log fields by role in every engine. Architecture: [Policy pushdown and open lineage](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/policy-and-lineage).
- **Investigation agents.** Let an agent query logs and draft incident timelines under strict tool policy. Architecture: [Governed AI agents for data engineering](https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/governed-ai-agents).

Canonical page: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures/industries/cybersecurity
